fields.subtitle: To Turn and Live
fields.description: Richard Baxter's plea to anyone who has not yet turned to Christ, built on God's oath in Ezekiel 33:11 — “why will ye die?” It reasons, answers objections and refuses to let a reader stay undecided. Written by a pastor who expected to give an account for every soul in his parish, it became one of the most widely circulated evangelistic books in English.

fields.title: A Short Account of the Author and the Great Success Which Attended the Call When First Published
fields.body_html:
A SHORT

ACCOUNT

OF

THE AUTHOR;

AND

The great Success which attended the CALL
when first published.

IT may be fitting to begin with an account of this book given by Mr. Baxter himself, which was found in his study after his death, in his own words:

“I published a short treatise on conversion, entitled A Call to the Unconverted. The occasion of it was my conversations with Bishop Ussher while I was in London. He approved my method and the directions I had given for peace of conscience, and pressed me hard to write directions suited to the different states of Christians, and also against particular sins. I revered the man, but paid little attention to these urgings, supposing I could do nothing that had not already been done better. But when he was dead, his words sank deeper into my mind, and I resolved to follow his advice; though with this difference, that for the first sort of people (the ungodly) I thought earnest persuasions more fitting than directions alone. And so for them I published this little book, which God has blessed with unexpected success, beyond all the rest I have written, except “The Saints’ Rest.” In a little more than a year about twenty thousand copies were printed with my consent, and about ten thousand since, besides many thousands in pirated editions, which poor men printed for the sake of profit.—Through God’s mercy, I have news of almost whole households converted by this small book, which I thought so little of. And as if all this in England, Scotland and Ireland were not mercy enough for me, God (since I was silenced) has sent it on his errand to many overseas; for when Mr. Eliot had printed the whole Bible in the Indian language, he next translated this “Call to the Unconverted” of mine, as he wrote to us here.—And God would make still further use of it; for Mr. Stoop, the pastor of the French Church in London, being driven from here by the displeasure of his superiors, was pleased to translate it into French. I hope it will not be unprofitable there, nor in Germany, when it is printed in Dutch.”

It may also be fitting to mention Dr. Bates’s account of the author and of this useful Treatise.—In his sermon at Mr. Baxter’s funeral he says: “His books of practical divinity have been effective in more conversions of sinners to God than any printed in our time, and while the church remains on earth they will go on working to recover lost souls.—There is a vigorous pulse in them that keeps the reader awake and attentive.”—His Call to the Unconverted, how small a book, but how powerful in its effect! Truth speaks in it with such authority and force that it makes the reader lay his hand on his heart and find that he has a soul and a conscience, though he lived before as if he had none. He told some friends that six brothers were converted by reading that Call, and that every week he received letters from people converted by his books. He said this with the most humble thankfulness that God was pleased to use him as an instrument for the salvation of souls.”

Self-denial and contempt for the world were shining graces in him. I never knew anyone less indulgent to himself, or more indifferent to his worldly interests.

His patience was truly Christian; he was tested by many afflictions. We are sensitive about our reputation. His name was hidden under a cloud of slander, and many scandalous darts were thrown at him. He was accused over his Paraphrase upon the New Testament and condemned, unheard, to prison, where he stayed for some years. Yet he was so far from being shaken by that unjust prosecution that he joyfully said to a faithful friend, “What more could I desire from God than, having served him as well as I could, to be called to suffer for him!”

His peaceable spirit was a clear mark that he was a child of God. How earnestly he worked to heal the divisions among us is publicly known. He said to a friend, “I can as willingly be a martyr for love as for any article of the creed.”—It is strange, even astonishing, that those who agree on the substantial and great points of the Reformed religion, and differ only in things that are less clear and of less importance than those they agree on, should belong to opposing parties.

Death reveals the secrets of the heart; then words are spoken with the most feeling and the least pretence. This excellent saint was the same in his life and in his death: his last hours were spent preparing others and himself to appear before God. He said to the friends who visited him, “You come here to learn to die. I am not the only person who must go this way. I can assure you that your whole life, however long it is, is little enough to prepare for death. Beware of this vain, deceitful world and the lusts of the flesh. Be sure you choose God for your portion, heaven for your home, God’s glory for your aim, his word for your rule, and then you need never fear but that we shall meet with comfort.”

Never was a penitent sinner more humble and self-abasing; never was a sincere believer more calm and comforted. He called himself the vilest dunghill-worm (it was his usual expression) that ever went to heaven. He marvelled at God’s condescension to man, saying, “Lord, what is man? What am I? A vile worm before the great God!” Many times he prayed, “God be merciful to me a sinner!” and blessed God that this prayer was left on record in the Gospel as one that was answered. He said, “God may justly condemn me for the best duty I ever did; and all my hopes are from the free mercy of God in Christ,” which he often prayed for.

After a sleep he woke and said, “I shall rest from my labour.” A minister who was there said, “And your works follow you.” He replied, “No works! I will leave out works, if God will grant me the other.”—When a friend was comforting him by reminding him of the good many had received from his preaching and writings, he said, “I was only a pen in God’s hand, and what praise is due to a pen?”

His submission to the will of God in his severe illness was outstanding. When extreme pain drove him to pray earnestly to God for release by death, he would check himself: “It is not fit for me to dictate,” and said, “When you will, what you will.”

At another time he said “that he found great comfort and sweetness in repeating the words of the Lord’s Prayer, and was sorry that some good people were prejudiced against using it; for all the petitions needed for soul and body were contained in it.”

At other times he gave excellent counsel to young ministers who visited him, prayed earnestly to God to bless their labours and make them very successful in converting many souls to Christ, and expressed great joy that they were of moderate and peaceable spirits.

During his illness, when he was asked how he was, his reply was, “Almost well.” His joy was most remarkable when, in his own judgment, death was nearest; and his spiritual joy was at last completed in eternal joy.

So lived and died that blessed saint.—I have given a sincere, short account of him, without any artificial invention of words. All our tears fall short of the grief such a priceless loss deserves. It is the comfort of his friends that he enjoys a blessed reward in heaven and has left a precious memory on earth.

Now blessed be the gracious God, that he was pleased to extend the life of his servant, so useful and beneficial to the world, to a full age, and that he has brought him slowly and safely to heaven.

I will close this account with my own considered wish: “May I live the rest of my life as wholly to the glory of God as he lived; and when I come to the end of my life, may I die in the same blessed peace in which he died; may I be with him in the kingdom of light and love for ever.”

I will also add Dr. Calamy’s account of this Treatise. His words are these: “In 1657 Mr. Baxter published a Call to the Unconverted, a book blessed by God with marvellous success in reclaiming people from their ungodliness. Twenty thousand copies were printed and distributed in little more than a year. It was translated into French and Dutch and other European languages; Mr. Eliot translated it into the Indian language; and Mr. Cotton Mather, in his life, gives an account of an Indian prince who was so moved by this book that he sat reading it, with tears in his eyes, until he died.”

fields.title: Preface
fields.body_html:
To all unsanctified people who read this book, especially my hearers in the borough and parish of Kidderminster.

Men and Brethren,

THE eternal God, who made you for an everlasting life and redeemed you by his only Son when you had lost it and yourselves, has been mindful of you in your sin and misery. He has written the gospel, sealed it by his Spirit, and commanded his ministers to preach it to the world, so that, with pardon freely offered to you and heaven set before you, he might call you away from your fleshly pleasures and from chasing after this deceitful world, and acquaint you with the life you were created and redeemed for, before you are dead and past remedy. He does not send you prophets or apostles who receive their message by direct revelation; but he still calls you by his ordinary ministers, who are commissioned by him to preach the same gospel that Christ and his apostles first delivered. The Lord sees how you forget him and your final end, and how lightly you treat everlasting things, like people who do not understand what they have to do or suffer. He sees how bold you are in sin, how unafraid of threatenings, how careless of your souls, and how the works of unbelievers are in your lives while the faith of Christians is in your mouths. He sees the dreadful day close at hand, when your sorrows will begin and you must lament all this with useless cries in torment and despair; and then the memory of your folly will tear your hearts, unless true conversion prevents it now. Out of compassion for your sinful, miserable souls, the Lord, who knows your case better than you can, has made it our duty to speak to you in his name (2 Cor. 5:19), and to tell you plainly of your sin and misery, what your end will be, and how sad a change you will soon see if you go on a little longer. Having bought you at so dear a price as the blood of his Son Jesus Christ, and having made you so free and general a promise of pardon, grace and everlasting glory, he commands us to offer all this to you as the gift of God, and to plead with you to consider how necessary and how valuable his offer is.—He sees you and pities you while you are drowned in worldly cares and pleasures, eagerly chasing childish toys, and wasting on a thing of nothing that short and precious time in which you should be getting ready for an everlasting life. So he has commanded us to call after you, to tell you how you are wasting your labour and are about to lose your souls, and to tell you what greater and better things you could certainly have if you would listen to his Call (Isa. 55:1, 2, 3). We believe and obey the voice of God, and come to you with his message; he has charged us to preach, to be urgent with you in season and out of season, to lift up our voice like a trumpet, and to show you your transgressions and your sins (Isa. 58:1; 2 Tim. 4:1, 2). But alas! to the grief of our souls and your own ruin, you stop your ears, stiffen your necks and harden your hearts, and send us back to God groaning, to tell him that we have delivered his message but can do you no good, and can scarcely get a sober hearing.—Oh, that our eyes were a fountain of tears, so that we might weep for our ignorant, careless people, who have Christ, and pardon, and life, and heaven set before them, and have no heart to know or value them! They might have Christ and grace and glory as well as others, if it were not for their wilful negligence and contempt! Oh, that the Lord would fill our hearts with more compassion for these miserable souls, so that we might throw ourselves at their very feet, follow them to their houses, and speak to them with our bitter tears! For we have long preached to many of them in vain. We work at plainness to make them understand, and many of them will not understand us; we work at serious, piercing words to make them feel, but they will not feel. If the greatest matters would work on them, we would wake them up; if the sweetest things would work, we would draw them and win their hearts; if the most dreadful things would work, we would at least frighten them out of their wickedness; if truth and certainty would take hold of them, we would soon convince them; if the God who made them and the Christ who bought them could be heard, their case would soon be changed; if Scripture could be heard, we would soon prevail; if reason, even the best and strongest reason, could be heard, we would not doubt that we would quickly convince them; if experience could be heard, even their own experience and the experience of all the world, the matter would be mended; indeed, if the conscience within them could be heard, things would be better with them than they are. But if nothing can be heard, what then shall we do for them? If the dreadful God of heaven is ignored, who then will be regarded? If the priceless love and blood of a Redeemer are made light of, what then will be valued? If heaven has no desirable glory for them, and everlasting joys are worth nothing; if they can joke about hell, dance around the bottomless pit and play with the consuming fire, even when God and man warn them of it; what shall we do for souls like these?

Once more, in the name of the God of heaven, I will deliver to you the message he has commanded us, and leave it in these lasting lines, to convert you or to condemn you; to change you, or to rise up in judgment against you and be a witness to your faces that you once had a serious call to turn. Hear, all you who are drudges of the world and servants of the flesh and Satan! You who spend your days chasing prosperity on earth, and drown your consciences in drinking, gluttony, idleness and foolish amusements; who know your sin and yet will sin, as if you defied God and told him to do his worst and spare nothing! Listen, all you who pay no attention to God, who have no heart for holy things and find no taste in the word or worship of the Lord, or in thinking or speaking of eternal life; who are careless of your immortal souls and never spend one hour asking what condition they are in, whether sanctified or unsanctified, and whether you are ready to appear before the Lord! Listen, all you who by sinning in the light have sinned yourselves into unbelief, and do not believe the word of God. Whoever has an ear to hear, let him hear the gracious and yet dreadful call of God! His eye has been on you all this while. Your sins are recorded, and you will certainly hear of them again. God keeps the book now, and he will write it all on your consciences with his terrors, and then you also will keep it yourselves. O sinners, if only you knew what you are doing, and whom you are offending all this while! The sun itself is darkness before that Majesty whom you abuse every day and carelessly provoke. The sinning angels could not stand before him, but were cast down to be tormented as devils. And do such feeble worms as you dare to offend so carelessly, and set yourselves against your Maker? Oh, if only you knew a little of the condition of that wretched soul who has set the living God against him! The words of the mouth of the one who made you can unmake you; the frown of his face will cut you off and throw you out into outer darkness. How eager the devils who have tempted you are to get their hands on you! They only wait for the word from God to take you and use you as their own; and then in a moment you will be in hell. If God is against you, all things are against you. This world is only your prison, however much you love it; you are only being kept in it for the day of wrath (Job 21:30). The Judge is coming; your soul is already on its way. A little while longer, and your friend will say of you, “He is dead;” and you will see the things you now despise, and feel what you now will not believe. Death will bring an argument you cannot answer, an argument that will thoroughly refute your quibbles against the words and ways of God and all your self-satisfied foolishness. And then how soon your mind will change! Be an unbeliever then, if you can; stand by all the words you used to speak against a holy and heavenly life. Make good that case then before the Lord, which you used to argue against your teachers and against the people who feared God. Stand by your old opinions then, and your contempt for the diligence of the saints; get your strongest reasons ready now, and stand up then before the Judge and plead like a man for your fleshly, worldly and ungodly life. But know that you will have someone to argue with who will not be stared down by you, nor put off as easily as we, your fellow creatures. O poor soul! There is nothing but a thin veil of flesh between you and that astonishing sight which will soon silence you, change your tune and make you think differently! As soon as death has drawn back this curtain, you will see at once what will quickly leave you speechless. And how soon that day and hour will come! When you have had only a few more merry hours, a few more pleasant drinks and mouthfuls, and a little more of the honours and riches of the world, your portion will be spent and your pleasures ended, and everything you set your heart on will be gone. Of all that you sold your Saviour and salvation for, nothing will be left but the heavy reckoning. Like a thief who sits merrily in an alehouse spending the money he has stolen while men are riding at full speed to arrest him, so it is with you. While you are drowned in cares or fleshly pleasures and making merry with your own shame, death is coming at full speed to seize you and carry your souls to a place and state you little know or think of now. Suppose that while you were bold and busy in your sin a messenger were riding hard from London to arrest you and take your lives. Though you could not see him, if you knew he was coming it would spoil your fun; you would be thinking of the speed he was making, and listening for his knock at your door. Oh, if only you could see what speed death is making, though he has not yet caught up with you! No courier is so swift! No messenger more sure! As surely as the sun will be with you in the morning, though it has many thousands and hundreds of thousands of miles to go in the night, so surely will death be with you soon; and then where is your sport and pleasure? Will you joke and bluster then? Will you jeer at those who warned you then? Then which is better, to be a believing saint or a sensual worldling? “And then whose shall all these things be” that you have gathered? (Luke 12:19, 20, 21). Do you not notice that days and weeks are quickly gone, and nights and mornings come fast and follow one another quickly? You sleep, “but your damnation slumbereth not;” you linger, “but your judgment this long time lingereth not” (2 Pet. 2:3, 4, 5), for which “you are reserved for punishment” (2 Pet. 2:8, 9).—“O that you were wise to understand this, and that you did consider your latter end” (Deut. 32:29).—“He that hath an ear to hear, let him hear the call of God in this day of his salvation.”

O careless sinners! If only you knew the love you so ungratefully neglect, and the preciousness of the blood of Christ which you despise! If only you knew the riches of the gospel! If only you knew, even a little, the certainty, the glory and the blessedness of that everlasting life which you will not set your hearts on now, nor be persuaded to seek first and diligently (Heb. 11:6 and 12:28; Matt. 6:12). If you only knew the endless life with God which you now neglect, how quickly you would throw away your sin! How quickly you would change your mind and life, your course and company, turn the streams of your affections and set your care on something else! How firmly you would refuse to give in to the temptations that now deceive you and carry you away! How zealously you would exert yourselves for that most blessed life! How earnest you would be with God in prayer! How diligent in hearing, learning and asking!—How serious in meditating on the laws of God! (Psa. 1:2). How afraid of sinning in thought, word or deed, and how careful to please God and grow in holiness!—Oh, what a changed people you would be! And why should the sure word of God, which opens these glorious and eternal things to you, not be believed by you and prevail with you?

Indeed, let me tell you that even here on earth you have little idea of the difference between the life you refuse and the life you would choose. The sanctified are talking with God when you hardly dare think of him, and when you are talking only with earth and flesh.—Their citizenship is in heaven when you are complete strangers to it, your belly is your god, and your mind is set on earthly things (Phil. 3:18, 19, 20). They are seeking the face of God when you seek nothing higher than this world.—They are busily preparing for an endless life, where they will be equal to the angels (Luke 20:36), while you are taken up with a shadow and a passing thing of nothing. How low and base your earthly, fleshly, sinful life is compared with the noble, spiritual life of true believers! Many times I have looked on such people with grief and pity, watching them trudge about the world and spend their lives, care and labour on nothing but a little food and clothing, a little fading money, fleshly pleasures or empty honours, as if they had nothing higher to think about.—What difference is there between the lives of these people and the beasts that perish, who spend their time working and eating and living only so that they may live? They do not taste the inward, heavenly pleasures which believers taste and live on.—I would rather have a little of the comfort that believers get from looking forward to their heavenly inheritance, even with all the scorn and suffering that comes with it, than have all your pleasures and treacherous prosperity. I would not have one of your secret gripes and pangs of conscience, and your dark and dreadful thoughts of death and the life to come, for all the world has ever done for you, or all you can reasonably hope it will do. If I were in your unconverted, carnal state, and knew what I know and believed what I now believe, I think my life would be a foretaste of hell. How often I would be thinking of the terrors of the Lord and of the dismal day that is hurrying on! Surely death and hell would always be before me. I would think of them by day and dream of them by night; I would lie down in fear, rise in fear and live in fear, in case death came before I was converted. I would have little happiness in anything I owned, little pleasure in any company, and little joy in anything in the world, as long as I knew I was under the curse and wrath of God. I would always be afraid of hearing that voice (Luke 12:20): “Thou fool, this night shall thy soul be required of thee.” And that fearful sentence would be written on my conscience (Isa. 48:22 and 57:21): “There is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked.”—O poor sinners! There is a more joyful life than this that you might live, if only you were truly willing to listen to Christ and come home to God. Then you could draw near to God with boldness, call him your Father, and trust him with your souls and bodies in comfort. If you look at the promises, you may say, They are all mine. If you look at the curse, you may say, From this I am delivered! When you read the law, you can see what you are saved from!—When you read the gospel, you can see the one who redeemed you, see the course of his love, his holy life and his sufferings, and trace him through his temptations, tears and blood in the work of your salvation. You can see death conquered and heaven opened, and your resurrection and glorification provided for in the resurrection and glorification of your Lord. If you look at the saints, you may say, “They are my brothers and companions.” If you look at the unsanctified, you may rejoice to think that you are saved from that state. If you look at the heavens, the sun and moon and countless stars, you may think and say, “My Father’s face is infinitely more glorious; it is higher things that he has prepared for his saints; that is only the outer court of heaven. The blessedness he has promised us is so much higher that flesh and blood cannot look on it.” If you think of the grave, you may remember that the glorified Spirit, a living Head and a loving Father are all so closely related to your dust that it cannot be forgotten or neglected, but will revive more surely than the plants and flowers in the spring; because the soul, which is the root of the body, is still alive, and Christ, who is the root of both, is alive.—Even death, the king of terrors, may be remembered and welcomed with joy, as the day of your deliverance from the remains of sin and sorrow, the day you believed in, hoped for and waited for, when you will see the blessed things you had heard of and find, by present joyful experience, what it was to choose the better part and to be a sincere, believing saint. What do you say, Sir? Is this not a more delightful life, to be assured of salvation and ready to die, than to live as the ungodly do, whose hearts are weighed down with overindulgence and drunkenness and the cares of this life, so that that day comes on them unawares? (Luke 21:34, 36). Could you not live a comfortable life, once you were made heirs of heaven and sure of being saved when you leave the world?—Oh, look around you, then, and think what you are doing, and do not throw away hopes like these for nothing at all. The flesh and the world can give you no such hopes or comforts.

And besides all the misery you bring on yourselves, you are a trouble to others as long as you are unconverted. You trouble magistrates, who must rule you by their laws; you trouble ministers by resisting the light and guidance they offer you. Your sin and misery are the greatest grief and trouble to them in the world.—You trouble the commonwealth and draw the judgments of God down on it. It is you who most disturb the holy peace and order of the churches and hinder our unity and reformation, and who are the shame and trouble of the churches you push into and of the places where you live.—Ah, Lord, how heavy and sad a case this is! Even in England, where the gospel abounds more than in any other nation in the world, where teaching is so plain and common and all the help we could want is at hand; when the sword has been cutting us down and judgment has run through the land like a fire; when deliverances have relieved us and so many wonderful mercies have bound us to God, to the gospel and to a holy life; after all this, our cities, towns and countryside abound with multitudes of unsanctified people and swarm with so much sensuality, as we see everywhere to our grief! One would have thought that after all this light, all this experience and all these judgments and mercies of God, the people of this nation would have joined together as one man to turn to the Lord. One would have thought they would have come to their godly teachers, lamented all their former sins and asked them to join in public humiliation, to confess those sins openly and beg the Lord’s pardon for them; and that they would have asked for instruction for the future and been glad to be ruled by the Spirit within and the ministers of Christ without, according to the word of God. One would think that after such reasoning and Scripture evidence as they hear, and after all these means and mercies, there would not be an ungodly person left among us, nor a worldling, nor a drunkard, nor a hater of reformation, nor an enemy of holiness, to be found in all our towns or countryside. Even if we are not all agreed about some ceremonies or forms of government, one would think that by now we would all have agreed to live a holy and heavenly life, in obedience to God, his word and his ministers, and in love and peace with one another.—But alas! How far our people are from this course! Most of them, in most places, set their hearts on earthly things and do not “seek first the kingdom of God and the righteousness thereof,” but look on holiness as an unnecessary thing. Their families do not pray, or else a few heartless, lifeless words must do instead of heartfelt, fervent, daily prayers [or perhaps only on the Lord’s Day in the evening]. Their children are not taught the knowledge of Christ and the covenant of grace, nor brought up in the nurture of the Lord, though they solemnly promised all this at their baptism.

They do not instruct their servants in the matters of salvation; as long as the work gets done, they do not care. There are more abusive words in their households than gracious words that build people up. How few the families are that fear the Lord, ask his word and his ministers how they should live and what they should do, are willing to be taught and ruled, and seek everlasting life in earnest! And those few whom God has made so happy are usually the laughing-stock of their neighbours. When we see some living in drunkenness, some in pride and worldliness, and most of them caring little for their salvation, though the case is glaring and beyond all dispute, yet they will hardly be convinced of their misery, and still more hardly be recovered and reformed. When we have done all we can to save them from their sins, we leave most of them as we found them. And if, according to the law of God, we put them out of the communion of the church after they have stubbornly rejected all our warnings, they rage at us as if we were their enemies, their hearts fill with malice against us, and they will sooner set themselves against the Lord and his laws, his church and his ministers than against their deadly sins. This is the sorrowful case of England. We have magistrates who support the ways of godliness; a happy opportunity for unity and reformation lies before us; faithful ministers long to see the church and the ordinances of God rightly ordered; but the power of sin in our people defeats almost everything. Almost nowhere can a faithful minister set up the unquestionable discipline of Christ, or keep the most scandalous, unrepentant sinners back from the communion of the church and from sharing in the sacraments, without most of the people railing at him and reviling him, as if these ignorant, careless souls were wiser than their teachers, or than God himself. And so, in the day of our visitation, when God calls on us to reform his church, though magistrates seem willing and faithful ministers seem willing, the mass of the people are still unwilling. They have so blinded themselves and hardened their hearts that even in these days of light and grace they are the stubborn enemies of light and grace, and will not be brought by the calls of God to see their folly and know what is for their good. Oh, that the people of England “knew at least in this their day the things that belong unto their peace, before they are hid from their eyes!” (Luke 19:42).

O foolish, miserable souls! (Gal. 3:1). Who has bewitched your minds into such madness and your hearts into such deadness that you should be such deadly enemies to yourselves, and go on so stubbornly towards damnation that neither the word of God nor the persuasions of men can change your minds, hold back your hands or stop you, until you are past remedy? Well, sinners! This life will not last for ever; this patience will not wait on you for ever. Do not think that you can abuse your Maker and Redeemer, serve his enemies, degrade your souls, trouble the world, wrong the church, insult the godly, grieve your teachers and hinder reformation, and all at no cost. You do not yet know what this must cost you, but you must soon know, when the righteous God takes you in hand; and he will deal with you in a different way from the sharpest magistrates or the plainest-speaking pastors, unless you prevent the everlasting torments by a sound conversion and a speedy obedience to the call of God. “He that hath an ear to hear, let him hear,” while mercy still has a voice to call.

One objection I find most common in the mouths of the ungodly, especially in recent years. They say, “We can do nothing without God; we cannot have grace if God will not give it to us; and if he will, we will turn quickly. If he has not predestined us and will not turn us, how can we turn ourselves or be saved? It is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth.” And so they think they are excused.

I have answered this before, and in this book; but let me say this much now.—1. Though you cannot cure yourselves, you can hurt and poison yourselves. It is God who must sanctify your hearts; but who corrupted them? Will you deliberately take poison because you cannot cure yourselves? I would think that should make you all the more careful to avoid it. You should take all the more care not to sin, if you cannot mend what sin spoils.—2. Though you cannot be converted without the special grace of God, you must know that God gives his grace in the use of the holy means he has appointed for that purpose; and common grace may enable you to refrain from your gross sins (as far as the outward act goes) and to use those means. Can you truly say that you do as much as you are able to do? Are you not able to walk past an alehouse door, or to stay away from the company that hardens you in sin? Are you not able to hear the word, and think about what you heard when you get home, and consider your own condition and everlasting things? Are you not able to read good books from day to day, or at least on the Lord’s Day, and to talk with those who fear the Lord? You cannot say you have done all you are able to do.—3. So you must know that you can forfeit the grace and help of God by your wilful sinning or negligence, even though you cannot turn to God without grace. If you will not do what you can, it is just for God to deny you the grace by which you might do more. 4. As for God’s decrees, you must know that they do not separate the end from the means, but tie them together. God never decreed to save anyone but the sanctified, nor to damn anyone but the unsanctified. God decrees just as truly whether your land will be barren or fruitful this year, and exactly how long you will live in the world, as he has decreed whether you will be saved or not. And yet you would think a man a fool who stopped ploughing and sowing and said, “If God has decreed that my ground will bear corn, it will bear it whether I plough and sow or not. If God has decreed that I will live, I will live whether I eat or not; and if he has not, eating will not keep me alive.” Do you know how to answer such a man, or not? If you do, then you know how to answer yourselves, for the case is the same: God’s decree is as absolute about your bodies as about your souls. If you do not, then try these conclusions on your bodies first, before you venture to try them on your souls. See first whether God will keep you alive without food or clothing, whether he will give you corn without tilling and labour, and whether he will bring you to your journey’s end without travelling or being carried. And if you get on well with this, then try whether he will bring you to heaven without your diligent use of the means, and sit down and say, We cannot sanctify ourselves.

Well, Sirs, I have only three requests to make of you, and then I am done.

First, that you will seriously read through this small Treatise (and if you have people in your households who need it, that you will read it to them again and again; and if those who fear God would go now and then to their ignorant neighbours and read this or some other book on this subject to them, they might be a means of winning souls). If we cannot persuade people to do so small a piece of work for their own salvation as to read short instructions like these, they think very little of themselves and will most justly perish.

Secondly, when you have read through this book, I would beg you to go off alone and ponder a little what you have read, and consider, as in the sight of God, whether it is not true, whether it does not touch your souls closely, and whether it is not time to look around you. I also beg you to go on your knees and plead with the Lord to open your eyes to understand the truth and turn your hearts to the love of God, and to ask him for all the saving grace you have neglected for so long, and to keep at it from day to day until your hearts are changed.—And with that, that you will go to your pastors (who are set over you to take care of the health and safety of your souls, as physicians do for the health of your bodies), ask them to direct you what course to take, and tell them about your spiritual condition, so that you may have the benefit of their advice and help as ministers.

Or, if you do not have a faithful pastor at home, make use of some other in so great a need.

Thirdly, once you have come to know your sin and misery, your duty and your remedy, by reading, thinking, prayer and the advice of a minister, do not delay. Immediately leave your sinful company and ways, turn to God and obey his call. As you love your souls, be careful not to go on against so loud a call of God and against your own knowledge and conscience, or it will go worse with you on the day of judgment than with Sodom and Gomorrah. Ask God, as someone who is willing to know the truth and will not deliberately cheat his own soul. Search the holy Scriptures daily, and see whether these things are so or not. Test impartially whether it is safer to trust heaven or earth; whether it is better to follow God or man, the spirit or the flesh; whether it is better to live in holiness or in sin; and whether an unsanctified state is safe for you to stay in one day longer. And when you have found out which is best, decide accordingly, and make your choice without any more fuss. If you will be true to your own souls and do not love everlasting torments, I beg you, as from the Lord, simply to take this reasonable advice. Oh, what happy towns and countryside, and what a happy nation we might have, if only we could persuade our neighbours to agree to so necessary a proposal! What joyful men all faithful ministers would be, if only they could see their people truly heavenly and holy! This would be the unity, the peace, the safety and the glory of our churches, the happiness of our neighbours and the comfort of our souls. How comfortably we would then preach pardon and peace to you, and give you the sacraments, which are the seals of peace to you! And with what love and joy we might live among you! At your deathbed, how boldly we might comfort and encourage your departing souls! And at your burial, how comfortably we might leave you in the grave, expecting to meet your souls in heaven and to see your bodies raised to that glory!

But if most of you still go on in a careless, ignorant, fleshly, worldly or unholy life, and all our desires and labours cannot prevail enough to keep you from deliberately damning yourselves, then we must imitate our Lord, who delights in those few who are jewels, and in the little flock that will receive the kingdom, while most reap the misery they have sown. In nature, excellent things are few. The world does not have many suns or moons; only a little of the earth is gold or silver. Princes and nobles are only a small part of the human race, and not many people in the world are learned, judicious or wise. So if, because the gate is narrow and the way very narrow, only a few find salvation, God will still have his glory and pleasure in those few. And when Christ comes with his mighty angels in flaming fire, taking vengeance on those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, his coming will be glorified in his saints and admired in all true believers (2 Thess. 1:7, 8, 9, 10).

And as for the rest: God the Father was pleased to create them, and God the Son did not disdain to bear the penalty of their sins on the cross, and did not judge such sufferings to be in vain, though he knew that by refusing the sanctifying work of the Holy Spirit they would finally destroy themselves. So we who are his ministers, even if these are not gathered in, do not judge our labour wholly lost. See Isa. 49:5.

Reader, I have finished with you (when you have read through this book), but sin has not yet finished with you (even those sins you thought were forgotten long ago), and Satan has not yet finished with you (though he is out of sight now), and God has not yet finished with you, because you will not be persuaded to finish with your deadly, reigning sin. I have written you this persuasion as one who is going into another world, where the things I speak of here are seen, and as one who knows that you must soon be there yourself. As you ever hope to meet me with comfort before the Lord who made us; as you ever hope to escape the everlasting plagues prepared for those who finally neglect salvation, and for all who are not sanctified by the Holy Spirit and do not love the communion of the saints as members of the holy catholic church; and as you ever hope to see the face of Christ the judge, and the majesty of the Father, with peace and comfort, and to be received into glory when you are turned out of this world naked: I beg you, I charge you, to hear and obey the Call of God, and to turn with determination so that you may live. But if you will not, even though you have no real reason for it except that you will not, I summon you to answer for it before the Lord, and I require you there to bear me witness that I gave you warning, and that you were not condemned for lack of a call to turn and live, but because you would not believe it and obey it; which must also be the testimony of

Your serious Monitor,

Dec. 11, 1657.

RICHARD BAXTER.

Ezek. 33:11.

Say to them, As I live, saith the Lord God, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live. Turn ye, turn ye, from your evil ways, for, why will ye die, O house of Israel?

IT has been an astonishing wonder to many people besides me to read in the holy Scripture how few will be saved, and that the greater part even of those who are called will be shut out of the kingdom of heaven for ever and tormented with the devils in eternal fire. Unbelievers do not believe this when they read it, and so they must feel it. Those who do believe it are forced to cry out with Paul (Rom. 11:33), “O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!” But nature itself teaches us all to lay the blame for evil deeds on those who do them. So when we see some heinous thing done, a sense of justice moves us to ask who did it, so that the evil of the deed may bring the evil of shame back on its author. If we saw a man killed and cut to pieces, we would immediately ask, “Oh! Who did this cruel deed?” If the town were deliberately set on fire, you would ask, “What wicked wretch did this?” So when we read that most people will be firebrands of hell for ever, we cannot help asking ourselves, How does this come about? Whose fault is it? Who is so cruel as to be the cause of such a thing as this? And we find few who will admit the guilt. Everyone indeed admits that Satan is a cause; but that does not settle the question, because he is not the principal cause. He does not force people to sin, but tempts them to it, and leaves it to their own wills whether they will do it or not. He does not carry people to an alehouse, force their mouths open and pour the drink in; nor does he hold them so that they cannot go to the worship of God; nor does he force their hearts away from holy thoughts. So it lies between God himself and the sinner: one of them must be the principal cause of all this misery, whichever it is, for there is no one else to put it on. And God disowns it; he will not take it on himself. And the wicked usually disown it; they will not take it on themselves. And this is the dispute that is dealt with here in my text.

The Lord complains of the people, and the people think it is God’s fault. The same dispute is dealt with in chapter 18, verse 25, where they plainly say “that the way of the Lord is not equal,” and God says “it is their ways that are not equal.” So here they say in verse 10, “If our transgressions and our sins be upon us, and we pine away in them, how shall we then live?” As if they were saying, If we must die and be miserable, how can we help it? As if it were not their fault but God’s. But God in my text clears himself of it. He tells them how they may help it if they will, and persuades them to use the means; and if they will not be persuaded, he lets them know that it is their own fault; and if this does not satisfy them, he will not hold back from punishing them on that account. It is he who will be their judge, and he will judge them according to their ways. They are no judges of him or of themselves, since they lack the authority, wisdom and impartiality. Nor will arguing with God serve their purpose or save them from the execution of the justice they grumble at.

The words of this verse contain: 1. God clearing himself of the blame for their destruction. He does this not by disowning his judgments and their execution according to that law, nor by giving them any hope that the law will not be carried out, but by declaring that it is not their death that he takes pleasure in, but rather their turning back so that they may live; and he confirms this to them by his oath. 2. An express exhortation to the wicked to turn back, in which God not only commands but persuades, and even stoops to reason the case with them: why will they die? The direct aim of his exhortation is that they may turn and live. The secondary or reserved aims, supposing this is not reached, are these two: first, to convince them by the means he used that it is not God’s fault if they are miserable; secondly, to convince them, from their obvious wilfulness in rejecting all his commands and persuasions, that it is their own fault, and that they die because they will die.

The substance of the text lies in the following observations.

Doctrine 1. It is the unchangeable law of God that wicked people must turn or die.

Doctrine 2. It is the promise of God that the wicked shall live, if they will only turn.

Doctrine 3. God takes pleasure in people’s conversion and salvation, but not in their death or damnation: he would rather they turned back and lived than went on and died.

Doctrine 4. This is a most certain truth, and because God would not have people question it, he has solemnly confirmed it to them by his oath.

Doctrine 5. The Lord repeats his commands and persuasions to the wicked to turn.

Doctrine 6. The Lord stoops to reason the case with them, and asks the wicked why they will die.

Doctrine 7. If after all this the wicked will not turn, it is not God’s fault that they perish but their own; their own wilfulness is the cause of their damnation; they die because they will die.

Having laid the text open before your eyes in these plain propositions, I will next say something about each of them in order, though briefly.

Doctrine 1. It is the unchangeable law of God that wicked people must turn or die.

If you will believe God, believe this: there are only these two ways for every wicked person, either conversion or damnation. I know the wicked will hardly be persuaded either that this is true or that it is fair. It is no wonder if the guilty quarrel with the law. Few people are inclined to believe what they would not want to be true, and fewer still want something to be true that they see is against them. But quarrelling with the law or with the judge will not save the criminal. Believing and heeding the law might have prevented his death; but denying it and accusing it will only hasten it. If it were otherwise, a hundred would bring their reasoning against the law for every one who would bring his reasoning to the law. And people would rather give their reasons why they should not be punished than hear the commands and reasons of their rulers, which require them to obey. The law was not made for you to judge, but so that you might be ruled and judged by it.

But if anyone is so blind as to venture to question either the truth or the justice of this law of God, I will briefly give you evidence of both which I think should satisfy a reasonable person.

First, if you doubt whether this is the word of God or not, besides a hundred other texts you may be satisfied by these few.—Matt. 18:3: “Verily I say unto you, except ye be converted and become as little children, ye cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven.”—John 3:3: “Verily, verily, I say unto you, except a man be born again he cannot see the kingdom of God.”—2 Cor. 5:17: “If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature; old things are passed away, behold, all things are become new.”—Col. 3:9, 10: “Ye have put off the old man with his deeds, and have put on the new man, which is renewed in knowledge, after the image of him that created him.”—Heb. 12:14: “Without holiness no man shall see God.”—Rom. 8:8, 9: “So, then they that are in the flesh cannot please God.”—“Now if any man have not the spirit of Christ, he is none of his.”—Gal. 6:15: “For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision availeth anything nor uncircumcision, but a new creature.”—1 Pet. 1:3: “According to his abundant grace he hath begotten us to a lively hope.”—Verse 23: “Being born again not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, by the word of God, which liveth and abideth for ever.”—1 Pet. 2:1, 2: “Wherefore laying aside malice, and all guile, and hypocrisies, and envies, and evil speaking: as new-born babes desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby.”—Psa. 9:17: “The wicked shall be turned into hell, and all the nations that forget God.”—Psa. 11:5: “And the Lord loveth the righteous, but the wicked his soul hateth.”

Just as I need not stop to explain these texts, which are so plain, so I think I need not add any more of the multitude that say the same. If you are someone who believes the word of God, here is already enough to satisfy you that the wicked must be converted or condemned. You have already been brought so far that you must either admit that this is true or say plainly that you will not believe the word of God. And once you come to that point, there is little hope for you. Look after yourselves as well as you can, for you probably will not be long out of hell. You would be ready to fly in the face of anyone who called you a liar; and yet do you dare to call God a liar? But if you tell God plainly that you will not believe him, do not blame him if he never warns you again, or if he abandons you and gives you up as hopeless. For what would be the point of warning you if you will not believe him? If he sent an angel from heaven to you, it seems you would not believe. For an angel can speak only the word of God; and if an angel brought you any other gospel, you are not to receive it, but to hold him accursed (Gal. 1:8). And surely no angel is to be believed before the Son of God, who came from the Father to bring us this teaching. If he is not to be believed, then none of the angels in heaven are to be believed. And if those are your terms with God, I will leave you until he deals with you in a more convincing way. God has a voice that will make you hear. Though he pleads with you to hear the voice of his gospel, he will make you hear the voice of his sentence of condemnation without pleading. We cannot make you believe against your will; but God will make you feel against your will.

But let us hear what reason you have for refusing to believe this word of God, which tells us that the wicked must be converted or condemned. I know your reason: it is that you think it unlikely that God would be so unmerciful. You think it cruel to damn people for ever for so small a thing as a sinful life. And this leads us to the second thing, which is to vindicate the fairness of God in his laws and judgments.

First, I think you will not deny that it is most fitting for an immortal soul to be ruled by laws that promise an eternal reward and threaten an endless punishment. Otherwise the law would not suit the nature of the subject, who will not be fully ruled by any lower means than the hopes or fears of everlasting things. It is the same with temporal punishment. If a law were made now that the most heinous crimes should be punished with a hundred years’ imprisonment, this might have some effect, as being equal to our lifetimes. But if there had been no other penalties before the Flood, when people lived eight or nine hundred years, it would not have been enough, because people would know they could have so many hundreds of years free of punishment afterwards. So it is in the present case.

2. I suppose you will admit that the promise of an endless and unimaginable glory is not unsuited to the wisdom of God or to man’s case. Why, then, should you not think the same of the threat of an endless and unspeakable misery?

3. When you find in the word of God that this is so and will be so, do you think you are fit to contradict that word?—Will you call your Maker to the dock and examine his word on a charge of falsehood? Will you attack him and judge him by the law of your own notions? Are you wiser, better and more righteous than he is? Must the God of heaven come to you to learn wisdom? Must infinite wisdom learn from folly, and infinite holiness be corrected by a selfish sinner who cannot keep himself clean for an hour? Must the Almighty stand in the dock before a worm? Oh, the horrible arrogance of senseless dust! Shall every mole, or clod, or dunghill accuse the sun of darkness and take it on itself to light up the world? Where were you when the Almighty made these laws, that he did not call you into his counsel? Surely he made them before you were born, without asking your advice, and you came into the world too late to reverse them. If you could have done so great a work, you should have stepped out of your nothingness and contradicted Christ when he was on earth, or Moses before him, or saved Adam and his sinful descendants from the threatened death, so that there might have been no need of Christ! And what if God withdraws his patience and his upholding of you, and lets you drop into hell while you are quarrelling with his word?—Will you believe then that there is no hell?

4. If sin is such an evil that it requires the death of Christ to atone for it, it is no wonder if it deserves our everlasting misery.

5. And if the sin of the devils deserved an endless torment, why not the sin of man as well?

6. And I think you should see that it is not possible for the best of people, much less for the wicked, to be competent judges of what sin deserves. Alas! We are both blind and biased. You can never fully know what sin deserves until you fully know the evil of sin; and you can never fully know the evil of sin until you fully know: 1. the excellence of the soul, which it deforms; 2. the excellence of holiness, which it wipes out; 3. the reason and excellence of the law, which it violates; 4. the excellence of the glory, which it despises; 5. the excellence and office of reason, which it tramples down; 6. no, nor until you know the infinite excellence, almightiness and holiness of the God against whom it is committed. When you fully know all these, you will fully know what sin deserves. Besides, you know that the offender is too biased to judge the law or the proceedings of the judge. We judge by feeling, which blinds our reason. We see in ordinary worldly matters that most people think the cause is right when it is their own, and that everything done against them is wrong; and the wisest, most just and impartial friends may try to persuade them otherwise, and it is all in vain. There are few children who do not think their father unmerciful, or hard on them, if he whips them. There is hardly a wretch so vile that he does not think the church wrongs him if it excommunicates him; and hardly a thief or murderer who is hanged who would not accuse the law and the judge of cruelty, if that would serve his purpose.

7. Can you think that an unholy soul is fit for heaven? Alas! Such people could not love God there, nor give him any service he could accept. They are contrary to God; they loathe what he loves most, and love what he abhors. They are incapable even of that imperfect communion with him which his saints share in here. How then can they live in that perfect love of him, and full delight and communion with him, which is the blessedness of heaven? You do not accuse yourselves of unmercifulness if you do not make your enemy your closest counsellor; and yet you will blame the absolute Lord, the most wise and gracious Sovereign of the world, if he condemns the unconverted to perpetual misery.

USE.

I beg all of you who love your souls, instead of quarrelling with God and with his word, to bow to it immediately and make good use of it. All you in this congregation who are unconverted, take this as the certain truth of God: before long you must be converted or condemned; there is no other way but to turn or die. When God, who cannot lie, has told you this; when you hear it from the Maker and Judge of the world, it is time for whoever has ears to hear. By now you may see what you have to rely on. You are nothing but dead and damned people unless you are converted. If I told you otherwise, I would be deceiving you with a lie.—If I hid this from you, I would ruin you and be guilty of your blood, as the verses before my text assure me (verse 8): “When I say to the wicked, O wicked man, thou shalt surely die, if thou dost not speak to warn the wicked from his way, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at thy hand.”—So you see that, though this is a rough and unwelcome teaching, it is one we must preach and you must hear. It is easier to hear of hell than to feel it. If your needs did not require it, we would not hurt your tender ears with truths that seem so harsh and painful. Hell would not be so full if people were only willing to know their condition and to hear and think about it. The reason so few escape it is that they do not strive to enter through the narrow gate of conversion and walk the narrow way of holiness while they have time. And they do not strive, because they are not awakened to a lively sense of the danger they are in. And they are not awakened, because they are unwilling to hear or think of it; and that is partly from foolish tenderness and carnal self-love, and partly because they do not really believe the word that threatens it.—Even if you will not wholly believe this truth, I think its weight should force you to remember it; it should follow you and give you no rest until you are converted. If you had heard this word just once by the voice of an angel, “You must be converted or condemned; turn or die,” would it not stick in your mind and haunt you night and day, so that in your sinning you would remember it, as if the voice were still in your ears, “Turn or die!”? Oh, how happy your souls would be if it might work on you like this, and never be forgotten or leave you alone until it had driven your heart home to God! But if you throw it out by forgetfulness or unbelief, how can it work for your conversion and salvation? But take this with you, to your sorrow: though you may put this out of your minds, you cannot put it out of the Bible. There it will stand as a settled truth, which you will know by experience for ever, that there is no other way but turn or die.

Oh, what is the matter, then, that the hearts of sinners are not pierced by so weighty a truth? You would think that every unconverted soul who hears these words would be cut to the heart and think, This is my own case, and never be at peace until they found themselves converted.—Believe me, Sirs, this drowsy, careless state will not last long. Conversion and condemnation are both awakening things. I can foretell it as truly as if I saw it with my eyes, that either grace or hell will soon bring these matters home to you and make you say, “What have I done? What a foolish, wicked course I have taken!” The scornful and stupid state of sinners will last only a little while. As soon as they either turn or die, the presumptuous dream will be over, and then their wits and feeling will return.

But I foresee two things that are likely to harden the unconverted and make me lose all my labour, unless they can be cleared out of the way: the misunderstanding of these two words, [the wicked] and [turn]. Some will think to themselves, It is true, the wicked must turn or die; but what is that to me? I am not wicked, though I am a sinner, as all people are. Others will think, “It is true that we must turn from our evil ways; but I turned long ago; I trust this is not still to be done.” And so, while wicked people think they are not wicked but are already converted, we lose all our labour in persuading them to turn. So before I go any further I will tell you here who is meant by the wicked, and who they are who must turn or die; and also what is meant by turning, and who are truly converted. I have deliberately kept this for this place, preferring the order that suits my purpose.

And here you may notice that, in the sense of the text, a wicked person and a converted person are opposites. No one who is converted is a wicked person, and no one who is wicked is a converted person; so to be a wicked person and to be an unconverted person are one and the same. And so in explaining one we will explain both.

Before I can tell you what either wickedness or conversion is, I must go to the bottom and bring the matter up from the beginning.

It pleased the great Creator of the world to make three kinds of living creatures.—He made angels pure spirits, without flesh, and so he made them only for heaven and not to live on earth. Beasts were made flesh, without immortal souls, and so they were made only for the earth and not for heaven. Man is of a middle nature between the two, sharing in both flesh and spirit; so he is made for earth, but as his passage or road to heaven, not so that this should be his home or his happiness. The blessed state man was made for was to see the glorious majesty of the Lord and praise him among his holy angels, and to love him and be filled with his love for ever. And as this was the end man was made for, so God gave him means fitted for reaching it. These means were mainly two: first, the right disposition of man’s mind; secondly, the right ordering of his life. For the first, God suited man’s disposition to the end, giving him such knowledge of God as was fit for his present state, and a heart inclined to God in holy love. But he did not fix or confirm him in this condition; having made him a free agent, he left him in the hands of his own free will. For the second, God did what belonged to him: he gave man a perfect law, requiring him to continue in the love of God and to obey him perfectly. By deliberately breaking this law, man not only forfeited his hopes of everlasting life, but also turned his heart from God and fixed it on these lower, fleshly things, and so blotted the spiritual image of God out of the soul. So man both fell short of the glory of God, which was his end, and put himself out of the way by which he should have reached it; and this both in the frame of his heart and in the course of his life. He lost the holy inclination and love of his soul towards God, and instead he took on an inclination and love for pleasing his flesh, or carnal self, by earthly things, growing a stranger to God and familiar with the creature. And the course of his life was suited to the inclination of his heart: he lived for his carnal self and not for God; he sought the creature to please his flesh, instead of seeking to please the Lord. With this nature, or corrupt inclination, we are all now born into the world; for “Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?” (Job 14:4). As a lion has a fierce and cruel nature before it devours anything, and an adder has a venomous nature before it stings, so in our infancy we have these sinful natures or inclinations before we think or speak or do anything wrong; and from this springs all the sin of our lives. And not only that: when God in his mercy has provided us a remedy, the Lord Jesus Christ, to be the Saviour of our souls and bring us back to God again, we naturally love our present state and are unwilling to be brought out of it, and so are set against the means of our recovery. And though custom has taught us to thank Christ for his goodwill, carnal self persuades us to refuse his remedies, and to ask to be excused when we are commanded to take the medicines he offers and are called to leave everything and follow him to God and glory.

I beg you, read this page over again and take note of it; for in these few words you have a true description of our natural state, and so of a wicked person. For everyone who is in this state of corrupted nature is a wicked person, and in a state of death.

This also prepares you to understand what it is to be converted. For that, you must further know that the mercy of God, unwilling that man should perish in his sin, provided a remedy. He caused his Son to take our nature, and, being God and man in one person, to become a mediator between God and man, and by dying for our sins on the cross to ransom us from the curse of God and the power of the devil. And having redeemed us in this way, the Father has delivered us into his hands as his own. On this basis the Father and the Mediator make a new law and covenant for man. It is not like the first, which gave life to no one but the perfectly obedient and condemned man for every sin. Christ has made a law of grace, a promise of pardon and everlasting life to all who are converted to God by true repentance and by faith in Christ. It is like an act of pardon made by a prince for a band of rebels, on condition that they lay down their arms, come in, and be loyal subjects from then on.

But the Lord knows that the human heart has grown so wicked that, for all this, people will not accept the remedy if they are left to themselves. So the Holy Spirit has taken it on himself as his office to inspire the apostles, to seal the Scriptures by miracles and wonders, and to enlighten and convert the elect.

So from this much you see that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit each have their own works, which are especially ascribed to them.

The Father’s works were to create us; to rule us as his rational creatures by the law of nature, and to judge us by it; and, in mercy, to provide us a Redeemer when we were lost, to send his Son and to accept his ransom.

The works of the Son for us were these: to ransom and redeem us by his sufferings and righteousness; to give out the promise or law of grace; to rule and judge the world as its Redeemer on terms of grace; to intercede for us, so that the benefit of his death may be passed on to us; and to send the Holy Spirit, which the Father also does by the Son. The works of the Holy Spirit for us are these: to write the holy Scriptures by inspiring and guiding the prophets and apostles, and sealing the word by his miraculous gifts and works; to enlighten and stir up the ordinary ministers of the gospel, and so enable and help them to publish that word; and by the same word to enlighten and convert human souls. So, just as you could not have been rational creatures if the Father had not created you, nor have had any access to God if the Son had not redeemed you, so you cannot have a part in Christ or be saved unless the Holy Spirit sanctifies you.

So by now you may see the various causes of this work. The Father sends his Son; the Son redeems us and makes the promise of grace; the Holy Spirit writes and seals this gospel; the apostles are the Spirit’s secretaries to write it down; the preachers of the gospel are to proclaim it and persuade people to obey it; and the Holy Spirit makes their preaching effective by opening people’s hearts to receive it. And all this is to restore the image of God in the soul, to set the heart on God again and take it off the creature and the carnal self to which it has defected, and so to turn the current of the life, which before was earthly, into a heavenly course; and all this by receiving Christ, the physician of the soul, by faith.

From what I have said you may see what it is to be wicked and what it is to be converted. I think it will be plainer still if I describe them by their several parts. For the first, a wicked person may be known by these three things.

First, he is someone who places his chief contentment on earth, who loves the creature more than God and his fleshly prosperity above heavenly happiness. He has a taste for the things of the flesh, but neither discerns nor has any taste for the things of the Spirit.—Though he will say that heaven is better than earth, he does not really value it that way for himself. If he could be sure of earth, he would let heaven go, and would rather stay here than be taken there. A life of perfect holiness in the sight of God, and in his love and praise for ever in heaven, does not appeal to his heart as much as a life of health, wealth and honour here on earth. And though he falsely claims to love God above all, he has never really felt the power of divine love within him; his mind is set more on the world or on fleshly pleasures than on God. In a word, whoever loves earth above heaven, and fleshly prosperity more than God, is a wicked, unconverted person.

On the other hand, a converted person is enlightened to see the loveliness of God, and believes the glory to be had with God so far that his heart is carried up to it and set on it more than on anything in this world. He would rather see the face of God, and live in his everlasting love and praise, than have all the wealth or pleasures of the world. He sees that everything else is vanity and that nothing but God can fill the soul; so, let the world go whichever way it will, he lays up his treasure and hopes in heaven, and for that he resolves to let everything go. As fire rises upwards, and the needle touched with the lodestone always turns to the north, so the converted soul is inclined to God. Nothing else can satisfy him, and he can find no contentment or rest except in God’s love. In a word, all who are converted value and love God more than all the world, and heavenly happiness is dearer to them than their fleshly prosperity. You may find proof of what I have said in these places of Scripture: Phil. 3:18, 21; Matt. 6:19, 20, 21; Col. 3:1, 2, 4, 5; Rom. 8:5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 18, 23; Psa. 73:25, 26.

Secondly, a wicked person is someone who makes it the main business of his life to prosper in the world and reach his fleshly goals. Though he may read and hear and do a good deal in the outward duties of religion, and keep away from disgraceful sins, all this is only on the side. He never makes it the main business of his life to please God and reach everlasting glory. He puts God off with the leftovers of the world, and gives him no more service than the flesh can spare; for he will not part with everything for heaven.

By contrast, a converted person is someone who makes it the main care and business of his life to please God and to be saved. He takes all the blessings of this life only as provisions for his journey towards another life, and uses the creature in subordination to God. He loves a holy life and longs to be more holy. He has no sin that he does not hate and long and pray and strive to be rid of. The drift and bent of his life is towards God; and if he sins, it is against the very bent of his heart and life, so he gets up again and grieves over it, and dares not deliberately live in any known sin. There is nothing in this world so dear to him that he cannot give it up to God and leave it for him and for the hope of glory.—You may see all this in Col. 3:1, 2, 3, 4, 5; Matt. 6:20, 33; Luke 18:22, 23, 29; Luke 14:18, 24, 26, 27; Rom. 8:13; Gal. 5:24; Luke 12:21, and so on.

Thirdly, the soul of a wicked person has never truly seen and tasted the mystery of redemption, nor thankfully welcomed the Saviour who is offered. He is not taken up with love for the Redeemer, nor willing to be ruled by him as the physician of his soul, so that he may be saved from the guilt and power of his sins and brought back to God. His heart is numb to this unspeakable benefit, and is entirely against the healing means by which he should be recovered. Though he may be willing to be religious in a carnal way, he never gives up his soul to Christ, and to the leading and guidance of his word and Spirit.

By contrast, the converted soul, having felt itself ruined by sin, and seeing that it has lost its peace with God and its hope of heaven and is in danger of everlasting misery, thankfully welcomes the news of redemption. Believing in the Lord Jesus as his only Saviour, he gives himself up to him for wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. He takes Christ as the life of his soul and lives by him, and uses him as a salve for every sore, marvelling at the wisdom and love of God in this wonderful work of man’s redemption. In a word, Christ dwells in his heart by faith, and the life he now lives is by faith in the Son of God, who loved him and gave himself for him; indeed, it is not so much he who lives as Christ in him. For these things, see Job 1:11, 12 and 3:20; John 15:2, 3, 4; 1 Cor. 1:20 and 2:2.

Now you see in plain terms, from the word of God, who are the wicked and who are the converted. Ignorant people think that if someone does not swear, curse, rail, get drunk, commit fornication or extort, and does not wrong anyone in his dealings; if he comes to church, says his prayers, receives the sacrament and sometimes reaches out his hand to relieve the poor, he cannot be unconverted. Or if someone who has been guilty of drunkenness, swearing, gambling or similar vices simply gives them up from now on, they think he is a converted person.—Others think that if someone who has been an enemy and scorner of godliness simply comes to approve of it, joins himself to the godly, and is hated by the wicked for it as the godly are, he must be a converted person. Some are so foolish as to think they are converted by taking up some new opinion. And some think that if they have only been frightened by the fear of hell, and have had conviction and torments of conscience, and on that account have intended and promised to reform, and have taken up a life of decent behaviour and outward religion, this must be true conversion. These are the poor deluded souls who are likely to lose the benefit of all our persuasions; and when they hear that the wicked must turn or die, they think this is not said to them, for they are not wicked but have already turned. That is why Christ told some of the rulers of the Jews, who were more serious and respectable than the common people, that “publicans and harlots go into the kingdom of Christ before them” (Matt. 21:31). Not that a harlot or gross sinner can be saved without conversion, but because it was easier to make these gross sinners see their sin and misery and the need for a change than the more respectable sort, who deceive themselves by thinking they are already converted when they are not.

O Sirs, conversion is a very different kind of work from what most people realise. It is no small matter to bring an earthly mind to heaven; to show a person the lovely excellence of God until he is taken up with a love for him that can never be put out; to break the heart for sin and make him flee for refuge to Christ and thankfully embrace him as the life of his soul; to have the very drift and bent of the heart and life changed, so that a person renounces what he took for happiness and places his happiness where he never placed it before, and does not live for the same end or pursue the same aim in the world as he used to. In a word, whoever is in Christ is a new creature: “old things are passed away, behold, all things are become new” (2 Cor. 5:17). He has a new understanding, a new will and resolve, new sorrows and desires and love and delight, new thoughts, new speech, new company (if possible) and a new way of life. Sin, which used to be a joking matter to him, is now so hateful and terrible to him that he flees from it as from death. The world, which was so lovely in his eyes, now appears to be only vanity and vexation. God, who was neglected before, is now the only happiness of his soul. Before, he was forgotten and every lust was preferred to him; but now he is set nearest the heart, and everything must give way to him; the heart is taken up with waiting on him and paying attention to him, is grieved when he hides his face, and never thinks itself well without him. Christ himself, who used to be thought of lightly, is now his only hope and refuge, and he lives on him as on his daily bread. He cannot pray without him, nor rejoice without him, nor think, nor speak, nor live without him.—Heaven itself, which he used to look on only as a tolerable fallback that he hoped might serve him better than hell when he could stay in the world no longer, is now taken as his home, the place of his only hope and rest, where he will see and love and praise the God who already has his heart. Hell, which used to seem only a bogeyman to frighten people away from sin, now appears to be a real misery, not to be risked or joked about.—The works of holiness, which he used to be weary of, and which seemed more fuss than was needed, are now both his recreation and his business, the trade he lives by. The Bible, which used to be almost like any ordinary book to him, is now the law of God, a letter written to him from heaven and signed with the name of the eternal Majesty. It is the rule of his thoughts and words and deeds; its commands are binding, its threats are dreadful, and its promises speak life to his soul. The godly, who seemed to him just like other people, are now the most excellent and happiest people on earth. And the wicked, who were his playmates, are now his grief; and he who could laugh at their sins is now more ready to weep for their sin and misery (Psa. 16:3 and 15:4; Phil. 3:18). In short, he has a new end in his thoughts and a new way in his efforts, and so his heart and life are new. Before, his carnal self was his end, and his pleasure, worldly profit and reputation were his way.
