Now God and everlasting glory are his end, and Christ, the Spirit, the word and the ordinances, holiness towards God, and righteousness and mercy towards people, are his way. Before, self was the chief ruler, to which the things of God and conscience had to bow and give way. Now God in Christ, by the Spirit, word and ministry, is the chief ruler, to whom both self and all the things of self must give way. So this is not a change in one, or two, or twenty points, but in the whole soul, and in the very end and bent of the way of life. A person may step out of one path into another and still have his face the same way, still going towards the same place. But it is another matter to turn right round and travel the opposite way, to an opposite place. So it is here. A person may turn from drunkenness to thrift, leave his drinking companions and other gross, disgraceful sins, and take up some duties of religion, and still be heading for the same end as before, aiming at his carnal self above all and still giving it the government of his soul. But when he is converted, this self is denied and taken down, and God is set up; his face is turned the opposite way; and he who before was devoted to himself and lived for himself is now, by sanctification, devoted to God and lives for God. Before, he asked himself what he should do with his time, his abilities and his property, and he used them for himself; but now he asks God what he should do with them, and uses them for him. Before, he would please God as far as was consistent with pleasing his flesh and carnal self, but not to their great displeasure. But now he will please God, however much the flesh and self are displeased. This is the great change God will make in all who will be saved.

You can say that the Holy Spirit is our sanctifier; but do you know what sanctification is? It is what I have now explained to you; and every man and woman in the world must have it, or be condemned to everlasting misery. They must turn or die.

Do you believe all this, or not? Surely you dare not say you do not, for it is beyond doubt or denial. These are not disputed questions, where one learned and godly person thinks one thing and another thinks another, where one party says this and another says that. Every denomination among us that deserves to be called Christian agrees with what I have said; and if you will not believe the God of truth, and that in a matter where every party believes him, you are utterly without excuse.

But if you do believe this, how is it that you live so quietly in an unconverted state? Do you know that you are converted? Can you find this wonderful change in your souls? Have you been born again and made new in this way?—Are these not strange things to many of you, things you have never felt in yourselves? Even if you cannot tell the day or week of your change, or the very sermon that converted you, do you find that the work is done; that there really is such a change, and that you have hearts like those described above? Alas! Most people go about their worldly business and trouble their minds very little with such thoughts. If they are only kept from scandalous sins and can say, “I am no whoremonger, nor thief, nor curser, nor swearer, nor tippler, nor extortioner; I go to church and say my prayers,” they think this is true conversion, and that they will be saved as well as anyone. Alas, this is foolish self-deception; it is too much contempt for an endless glory, and too gross a neglect of your immortal souls.—Can you make so light of heaven and hell? Your bodies will soon lie in the dust, and angels or devils will at once seize your souls; and every man and woman of you will soon be in other company and in another condition than you are now. You will live in those houses only a little longer; you will work in your shops only a little longer; you will sit in these seats and live on this earth only a little longer; you will see with those eyes, hear with those ears and speak with those tongues only a little longer, until the resurrection day. And can you manage to forget this? Oh, what a place of joy or torment you will soon be in! Oh, what a sight you will soon see in heaven or hell! Oh, what thoughts will soon fill your hearts with unspeakable delight or horror! What work you will be employed in: praising the Lord with saints and angels, or crying out with devils in unquenchable fire! And should all this be forgotten? And all this will be endless, sealed by an unchangeable decree. ETERNITY, ETERNITY will be the measure of your joys or sorrows. Can this be forgotten? And all this is true, most certainly true.—When you have gone up and down a little longer, and slept and woken a few more times, you will be dead and gone, and will find everything I tell you now to be true. And can you still forget it so completely now? Then you will remember that you heard this sermon, and that on this day, from this place, you were reminded of these things; and you will see that they are matters a thousand times greater than either you or I could have imagined. And should they be so completely forgotten now?

Dear friends, if the Lord had not awakened me to believe these things and take them to heart myself, I would have stayed in a dark and selfish state and perished for ever. But if he has truly made me feel them, it will compel me to have compassion on you as well as on myself. If your eyes were opened far enough to see hell, and you saw your unconverted neighbours dragged there with hideous cries, though they were people you thought of as honest on earth and who feared no such thing for themselves, such a sight would make you go home and think about it, and think again, and would make you warn everyone around you, as that damned worldling in Luke 16:28 wanted his brothers warned, so that they would not come to that place of torment. Faith is a kind of sight; it is the eye of the soul, the evidence of things not seen. If I believe God, it is next to seeing; so I beg you to excuse me if I am even half as earnest with you about these things as if I had seen them. If I were to die tomorrow, and it were in my power to come back from another world and tell you what I had seen, would you not be willing to hear me? Would you not believe and heed what I told you? If I could preach one sermon to you after I am dead and have seen what is done in the world to come, would you not want me to speak the truth plainly, and would you not crowd in to hear me, and take it to heart? But this must not be. God has his appointed way of teaching you by Scripture and ministers, and he will not indulge unbelievers so far as to send people from the dead to them and change his established way. If anyone quarrels with the sun, God will not indulge him so far as to set up a clearer light. Friends, I beg you, listen to me now as you would if I came to you from the dead; for I can give you as full assurance of the truth of what I say as if I had been there and seen it with my eyes. For it is possible for someone from the dead to deceive you; but Jesus Christ can never deceive you.—The word of God, delivered in Scripture and sealed by the miracles and holy workings of the Spirit, can never deceive you. Believe this, or believe nothing. Believe and obey this, or you are ruined. Now, as you ever believe the word of God, and as you ever care about the salvation of your souls, let me make this reasonable request of you, and I beg you not to refuse me: that without any more delay, when you have gone from here, you remember what you heard and begin an earnest search of your hearts, and say to yourselves: “Is it really so? Must I turn or die? Must I be converted or condemned? Then it is time for me to look around me, before it is too late. Oh, why did I not see to this until now? Why did I so recklessly put off so great a business? Was I awake, or in my right mind? O blessed God, what a mercy it is that you did not cut off my life all this while, before I had any sure hope of eternal life!—Well, God forbid that I should neglect this work any longer. What state is my soul in? Am I converted, or not? Has such a change or work ever been done in my soul? Have I been enlightened by the word and Spirit of the Lord to see the hatefulness of sin, the need of a Saviour, the love of Christ, and the excellence of God and glory? Is my heart broken and humbled within me for my former life? Have I thankfully welcomed my Saviour and Lord, who offered himself with pardon and life for my soul? Do I hate my former sinful life, and the remains of every sin in me? Do I flee from them as my deadly enemies? Do I give myself up to a life of holiness and obedience to God? Do I love it and delight in it? Can I truly say that I am dead to the world and to my carnal self, and that I live for God and the glory he has promised? Does heaven have more of my esteem and resolve than earth? And is God the dearest and highest in my soul? Once, I am sure, I lived mainly for the world and the flesh, and God had nothing but some heartless services which the world could spare, the leftovers of the flesh.—Is my heart now turned another way? Do I have a new aim, a new end, and a new set of holy affections? Have I set my hopes and heart on heaven? And is it not the scope, aim and bent of my heart and life to get safely to heaven, to see the glorious face of God, and to live in his everlasting love and praise? And when I sin, is it against the settled bent and aim of my heart? Do I conquer all gross sins, and am I weary of my weaknesses and willing to be rid of them? This is the state of a converted soul, and it must be so with me, or I must perish. Is it really so with me, or not? It is time to settle this doubt, before the dreadful Judge settles it. I am not such a stranger to my own heart and life that I cannot see something of whether I am converted like this or not. If I am not, it will do me no good to flatter my soul with false notions and hopes. I am resolved not to deceive myself any more, but to try to know truly, one way or the other, whether I am converted, yes or no; so that, if I am, I may rejoice in it, glorify my gracious Lord and go on in comfort until I reach the crown; and if I am not, I may set myself to beg and seek the grace that would convert me, and may turn without any more delay.—For if I find in time that I am off the way, by the help of Christ I may turn and be recovered; but if I wait until either my heart is abandoned by God to blindness or hardness, or until I am snatched away by death, it is too late then. There is no room for repentance and conversion then; I know it must be now or never.”

Sirs, this is my request to you: that you will take your hearts to task and examine them like this, until you see, if possible, whether you are converted or not. And if you cannot find it out by your own efforts, go to your ministers, if they are faithful and experienced men, and ask for their help. The matter is great; do not let shyness or carelessness hold you back. They are set over you to advise you for the saving of your souls, as physicians advise you for the curing of your bodies. It ruins many thousands that they think they are on the way to salvation when they are not, and think they are converted when it is no such thing. And then, when we call to them to turn, they go away as they came, and think this does not concern them, for they have already turned, and they hope they will do well enough in the way they are in, at least if they only pick the cleanest path and avoid some of the dirtiest steps. And alas! All the while they are living only for the world and the flesh, are strangers to God and eternal life, and are entirely off the way to heaven. And all this is largely because we cannot persuade them to give a few serious thoughts to their condition and spend a few hours examining their state. Is there not many a self-deceiving wretch hearing me today who has never spent one hour in all his life examining his soul and testing whether he is truly converted or not?—O merciful God, who cares for wretches who care no more for themselves, and does so much to save them from hell and help them to heaven when they will do so little for it themselves! If all who are on the way to hell only knew it, they would not dare to stay on it. The devil’s greatest hope of bringing you to damnation without rescue is to keep you blindfolded and ignorant of your state, and make you believe that you may do well enough in the way you are in. If you knew that you were off the way to heaven, and would be lost for ever if you died as you are, would you dare to sleep another night in the state you are in? Would you dare to live another day in it? Could you laugh heartily or be merry in such a state? What! And not knowing whether you may be snatched away to hell within an hour! Surely it would compel you to leave your former company and course and take up the ways of holiness and the communion of saints. Surely it would drive you to cry to God for a new heart, and to seek help from those who are fit to counsel you. Surely there is none of you who does not care about being damned. Well then, I beg you, examine your hearts at once, and give them no rest until you find out your condition; so that, if it is good, you may rejoice in it and go on; and if it is bad, you may at once look around you for recovery, as people who believe they must turn or die. What do you say, Sirs? Will you resolve and promise to take this much trouble for your own souls? Will you set about this self-examination when you get home? Is my request unreasonable? Your consciences know it is not.—Resolve on it, then, before you move, knowing how much it concerns your souls. I beg you, for the sake of the God who commands you, at whose judgment seat you will all soon appear, not to refuse me this reasonable request. For the sake of souls that must turn or die, I beg you not to refuse me: only make it your business to understand your own condition, build on sure ground, and know, one way or the other, whether you are converted or not, and do not risk your souls on careless complacency.

fields.title: Sermon II
fields.body_html:
Ezek. 33:11.

Say to them, As I live, saith the Lord God, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live. Turn ye, turn ye, from your evil ways, for, why will ye die, O house of Israel?

A TRUE description of those who are in a converted state has already been given you; the change that conversion makes in the soul has also been described; and the request has been repeated to you most earnestly, to consider your condition impartially and thoroughly. Do not rest satisfied until you know whether you are really converted.

But perhaps you will say, What if we find that we are still unconverted? What shall we do then?—This question leads me to my second doctrine, which will go a long way towards answering it, and to which I now turn.

Doctrine 2. It is the promise of God that the wicked shall live, if they will only turn; turn sincerely and thoroughly.

The Lord declares here that this is what he takes pleasure in: that the wicked turn and live. Heaven is made as sure to the converted as hell is to the unconverted. Turn and live is as certain a truth as turn or die. God was not bound to provide us a Saviour, or open a door of hope to us, or call us to repent and turn once we had thrown ourselves away by sin; but he has freely done it to magnify his mercy. Sinners, none of you will have reason to go home and say that I preach despair to you. Do we make a practice of shutting the door of mercy against you? Oh, that you would not shut it against yourselves! Do we make a practice of telling you that God will have no mercy on you even if you turn and are sanctified? When did you ever hear a preacher say such a thing? You who snarl at preachers of the gospel for wanting to keep you out of hell, and say that they preach despair, tell me, if you can, when you ever heard any sober man say that there is no hope for you even if you repent and are converted. No, it is the opposite that we proclaim from the Lord: whoever is born again, and by faith and repentance becomes a new creature, will certainly be saved. And we are so far from persuading you to despair of this that we urge you not to doubt it at all. Life, not death, is the first part of our message to you. Our commission is to offer salvation, certain salvation, a speedy, glorious, everlasting salvation, to every one of you: to the poorest beggar as well as the greatest lord; to the worst of you, even to drunkards, swearers, worldlings and thieves, and even to those who despise and insult the holy way of salvation. We are commanded by the Lord our Master to offer you a pardon for all that is past, if you will only now at last turn back and live. We are commanded to beg and plead with you to accept the offer and turn back; to tell you what provision Christ has made, what mercy is waiting for you, what patience waits on you, what kind thoughts God has towards you, and how happy, how certainly and unspeakably happy, you may be if you will.—We do also have a message of wrath and death, indeed of a twofold wrath and death; but neither is our main message. We must tell you of the wrath that is on you already, and the death you are born under for breaking the law of works; but this is only to show you your need of mercy and to stir you to value the grace of the Redeemer. And we tell you nothing but the truth, which you must know. For who will look for medicine if he does not know he is sick? It is not our telling you of your misery that makes you miserable; it drives you out to seek mercy. It is you who have brought this death on yourselves. We also tell you of another death, a far greater torment without remedy, which will fall on those who will not be converted. But, though this is true and must be told you, it is only the last and saddest part of our message. We are first to offer you mercy if you will turn; and it is only to those who will not turn, nor hear the voice of mercy, that we must foretell damnation. If you will only throw away your transgressions, delay no longer, come away at the call of Christ, be converted and become new creatures, we have not one word of damning wrath or death to speak against you.—Here, in the name of the Lord of life, I proclaim to all of you who hear me today, to the greatest and the oldest sinner, that you may have mercy and salvation if you will only turn. There is mercy in God; there is sufficiency in the satisfaction of Christ; the promise is free and full and universal; you may have life if you will only turn. But then, as you love your souls, remember what turning it is that Scripture speaks of. It is not patching up the old house, but pulling it all down and building again on Christ, the rock and sure foundation. It is not mending something in a carnal course of life, but putting the flesh to death and living by the Spirit. It is not serving the flesh and the world in a more reformed way, without any scandalous or disgraceful sins and with a certain kind of religiousness. It is changing your master, your works and your end, setting your face the opposite way, doing everything for the life you have never seen, and dedicating yourselves and all you have to God. This is the change that must be made if you want to live.

You yourselves are witnesses now that it is salvation, not damnation, that is the great teaching I preach to you, and the first part of my message to you. Accept this, and we will go no further with you; for we would not even frighten or trouble you with the name of damnation unless we had to.

But if you will not be saved, there is no help for it: damnation must follow; for there is no middle place between the two. You must have either life or death.

And we are not only to offer you life, but to show you the grounds on which we do it, and to call you to believe that God really means what he says; that the promise is true and extends to you, on its condition, as well as to others; and that heaven is no fancy but a real happiness.

If you ask, Where is your commission for this offer? Out of a hundred texts of Scripture, I will show it to you in these few.

First, you see it here in my text and the verses that follow, and in Ezekiel 18, as plainly as it can be spoken. And in 2 Cor. 5:17, 18, 19, 20, 21 you have the very sum of our commission: “If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature; old things passed away, behold, all things are become new. And all things are from God, who hath reconciled us unto himself by Jesus Christ, and hath given to us the ministry of reconciliation; to wit, that God was in Christ reconciling the world unto himself, not imputing their trespasses to them; and hath committed unto us the word of reconciliation: now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us, we pray you, in Christ’s stead, be ye reconciled unto God; for, he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin, that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.” So also Mark 16:15, 16: “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature. He that believeth (that is, with such a converting faith as is described) and is baptized, shall be saved: but he that believeth not shall be damned.” And Luke 24:46, 47: “Thus it behoved Christ to suffer, and rise from the dead the third day, and that repentance (which is conversion) and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations.” And Acts 5:30, 31: “The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom ye slew and hanged on a tree: him hath God exalted with his right hand, to be a Prince and a Saviour, to give repentance to Israel, and forgiveness of sins.” And Acts 13:38, 39: “Be it known unto you, therefore, men and brethren, that through this name is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins; and, by him, all that believe are justified from all things, from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses.” And in case you think this offer is limited to the Jews, see Gal. 6:15: “For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision, but a new creature.” And Luke 14:17: “Come, for all things are now ready;” and verses 23, 24.

By now you see that we are commanded to offer life to all of you, and to tell you from God that if you will turn, you may live.

Here you may safely trust your souls. For the love of God is the fountain of this offer (John 3:16), and the blood of the Son of God has bought it. The faithfulness and truth of God are pledged to make the promise good; miracles have sealed its truth; preachers are sent through the world to proclaim it; the sacraments are instituted and used for the solemn handing over of the mercy offered to those who will accept it; and the Spirit opens the heart to receive it, and is himself the pledge of full possession. So its truth is beyond dispute: the worst of you, and every one of you, if you will only be converted, may be saved.

Indeed, if you insist on believing that you will be saved without conversion, then you believe a falsehood; and if I preached that to you, I would be preaching a lie. That would not be believing God, but the devil and your own deceitful hearts.—God has his promise of life, and the devil has his promise of life. God’s promise is, “Turn back and live.” The devil’s promise is, “You shall live, whether you turn or not.”—The word of God is, as I have shown you, “Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18:3). “Except a man be born again, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God” (John 3:3, 5). “Without holiness none shall see God” (Heb. 12:14).—The devil’s word is, “You may be saved without being born again and converted; you may do well enough without being holy; God is only frightening you; he is too merciful to do what he says; he will be better to you than his word.”—And, alas! the greater part of the world believes this word of the devil before the word of God, just as our sin and misery came into the world. God said to our first parents, “If ye eat ye shall die.” And the devil contradicted him and said, “You shall not die, if you only cry ‘God have mercy’ at the end, and give up the acts of sin when you can practise them no longer.” And this is the word the world believes.—Oh, heinous wickedness, to believe the devil before God!

And yet that is not the worst. They blasphemously call this believing and trusting in God, when they put him in the shape of Satan, who was a liar from the beginning. When they believe that the word of God is a lie, they call it trusting God, and say they believe in him and trust in him for salvation. Where did God ever say that the unregenerate, unconverted and unsanctified will be saved? Show me such a word in Scripture; I challenge you to, if you can. This is the devil’s word, and to believe it is to believe the devil; it is the sin commonly called presumption. And do you call this believing and trusting God? There is everything in the word of God to comfort and strengthen the hearts of the sanctified, but not one word to strengthen the hands of wickedness, or to give anyone the least hope of being saved if they are never sanctified.

But if you will turn and come into the way of mercy, the mercy of the Lord is ready to welcome you. Then trust God boldly for salvation, for he has pledged his word to save you. He will be a Father to none but his children, and he will save none but those who forsake the world, the devil and the flesh, and come into his family to be members of his Son and have communion with his saints. But if they will not come in, it is their own fault. His doors are open; he keeps no one back. He never sent such a message as this to any of you: “It is too late now; I will not receive you, even if you are converted.”—He could have done so and done you no wrong; but he did not, and he does not to this day. He is still ready to receive you, if only you were ready to turn sincerely and with all your hearts. And the fullness of this truth will appear still more in the next two doctrines, which I will therefore go on to next, before I apply this any further.

Doctrine 3. God takes pleasure in people’s conversion and salvation, but not in their death or damnation. He would rather they turned and lived than went on and died.

I will first teach you how to understand this, and then make its truth clear to you.

For the first, you must note the following things.

1. A simple willingness, or delight, is the first act of the will, following the simple apprehension of the understanding, before it goes on to compare things with one another. But the choosing act of the will comes after, and presupposes the comparing, practical act of the understanding. And these two acts may often be directed to opposite objects without any fault at all in the person.

2. A sincere willingness may have various degrees. Some things I am willing for so far that I will do everything in my power to bring them about. And some things I truly want another person to do, when I still will not do everything I possibly can to obtain them, since I have many reasons that dissuade me, though I will still do all that belongs to me to do.

3. The will of a ruler, as ruler, is shown in making and enforcing laws; but the will of a person in his simple natural capacity, or as absolute owner of what is his, is shown in desiring or deciding on events.

4. A ruler’s will as lawgiver is first and chiefly that his laws be obeyed, and not at all that the penalty be carried out on anyone, except on the supposition that they will not obey his laws. But a ruler’s will as judge presupposes that the law has already been either kept or broken, and so he decides on rewards or punishments accordingly.

Having laid out these necessary distinctions, I will next apply them to the case in hand in the following propositions.

1. In this life we must know God in the mirror of his word and his creatures. So, in keeping with human nature, we ascribe understanding and will to him, removing all the imperfections we can, because we are capable of no higher positive conceptions of him.

2. And on the same grounds we distinguish (as Scripture does) between the acts of God’s will as they vary according to their relations or objects, though in God’s essence they are all one.

3. And we do so all the more boldly because, when we speak of Christ, we have more ground for it from his human nature.

4. And so we say that the simple delight, will or love of God reaches to all that is naturally or morally good, according to the nature and degree of its goodness. And so he takes pleasure in the conversion and salvation of all, which nevertheless will never come about.

5. And God, as ruler and lawgiver of the world, has a practical will for their salvation to this extent: he makes them a free deed of gift of Christ and life, and an act of pardon for all their sin, provided they do not ungratefully reject it; and he commands his messengers to offer this gift to all the world and persuade them to accept it. And so, as lawgiver and promiser, he does all that belongs to him to do for their salvation.

6. Yet as lawgiver he decrees that those who will not turn shall die; and as judge, when their day of grace is past, he will carry out that decree.

7. So he sincerely wills the conversion of those who will never be converted; but not as absolute Lord, with the fullest effective resolve, nor as something he decrees shall certainly come about, or would commit all his power to accomplish. It is in a prince’s power to set a guard on a would-be murderer to see that he does not commit murder and hang for it. But if for good reasons he does not do this, and only sends to his subjects to warn them and plead with them not to be murderers, I trust he may well say that he would not have them murder and be hanged. He takes no pleasure in it, but would rather they held back and lived. And if he does more for some, for some special reason, he is under no obligation to do so for all. The king may well say to all the murderers and felons in the land, “I have no pleasure in your death, but would rather you obeyed my laws and lived. But if you will not, I have decreed, for all that, that you shall die.”—The judge may truly say to the thief or murderer, “Alas, man, I take no delight in your death; I would rather you had kept the law and saved your life. But since you have not, I must condemn you, or else I would be unjust.” So, though God has no pleasure in your damnation, and therefore calls on you to turn back and live, he does have pleasure in displaying his own justice and carrying out his laws; and so, for all this, he has fully decreed that if you will not be converted, you will be condemned. If God were so much against the death of the wicked that he was resolved to do everything he could to prevent it, then no one would be condemned; whereas Christ tells you that few will be saved. But God is against your damnation to this extent: he will teach you and warn you, set life and death before you and give you your choice, and command his ministers to plead with you not to damn yourselves but to accept his mercy; and so he leaves you without excuse. But if this will not do, and you are still unconverted, he declares to you that he is resolved on your damnation, and has commanded us to say to you in his name (verse 8), “O wicked man, thou shalt surely die!” And Christ has all but sworn it again and again, with a “Verily, verily, except you be converted, and born again, ye cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18:3; John 3:3). Notice that he said, you cannot. It is useless to hope for it, and useless to dream that God is willing for it, for it is a thing that cannot be.

In a word, then, you see the meaning of the text: God, the great lawgiver of the world, takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but would rather they turned and lived; and yet he is resolved that none shall live but those who turn. As judge he even delights in justice and in showing his hatred of sin, though not in the misery they have brought on themselves, considered in itself.

2. As for the proofs of the point, I will be very brief with them, because I suppose you already believe it easily.

1. The very gracious nature of God, proclaimed in Exod. 34:6 and 20:6 and often elsewhere, may assure you of this, that he has no pleasure in your death.

2. If God had more pleasure in your death than in your conversion and life, he would not have commanded you so often in his word to turn; he would not have made you such promises of life if you will only turn; he would not have urged you to it with so many reasons. The whole tenor of his gospel proves the point.

3. And the commission he has given to the ministers of the gospel fully proves it. If God had taken more pleasure in your damnation than in your conversion and salvation, he would never have charged us to offer you mercy and teach you the way of life, both publicly and privately; to plead with you and beg you to turn and live; to make you aware of your sins and warn you of your danger; to do everything we possibly can for your conversion; and to keep patiently on doing it, even if you hate or abuse us for our trouble. Would God have done this, and appointed his ordinances for your good, if he took pleasure in your death?

4. It is proved also by the course of his providence. If God would rather you were damned than converted and saved, he would not back up his word with his works, draw you to himself by his daily kindness, and give you all the mercies of this life, which are his means to lead you to repentance (Rom. 2:4); nor would he bring you so often under his rod to force you to your senses. He would not set so many examples before your eyes; no, nor wait on you as patiently as he does, from day to day and year to year. These are not the signs of one who takes pleasure in your death.—If this had been his delight, how easily he could have had you in hell long ago! How often before now he could have snatched you away in the middle of your sins, with a curse or an oath or a lie in your mouth, in your ignorance, pride and sensuality! When you were last drunk, or last mocking the ways of God, how easily he could have stopped your breath, tamed you with his plagues and made you sober in another world! Alas! How small a thing it is for the Almighty to rule the tongue of the most profane railer, tie the hands of the most malicious persecutor, or calm the fury of the bitterest of his enemies, and make them know that they are only worms! If he frowned on you, you would drop into your grave. If he commissioned one of his angels to go and destroy ten thousand sinners, how quickly it would be done! How easily he can lay you on a sickbed and make you lie there roaring in pain, make you eat the insulting words you have spoken against his servants, his word, his worship and his holy ways, and make you send to beg the prayers of those you despised in your presumption! How easily he can lay your flesh under gripes and groans, make it too weak to hold your soul, and make it more loathsome than the dung of the earth!—That flesh which must now have what it loves, and must not be displeased though God is displeased, and must be humoured in food, drink and clothes whatever God says to the contrary: how quickly the frowns of God would consume it!—When you were passionately defending your sin, quarrelling with those who would have drawn you away from it, venting your spite on the one who rebuked you, and pleading for the works of darkness, how easily God could have snatched you away in a moment and set you before his dreadful Majesty, where you would see ten thousand times ten thousand glorious angels waiting at his throne; and called you there to plead your case, and asked you, “What have you to say now against your Creator, his truth, his servants or his holy ways? Plead your case now, and make the best of it you can. What can you say now to excuse your sins? Give an account now of your worldliness and fleshly life, of your time, and of all the mercies you have had!” Oh, how your stubborn heart would have melted, your proud looks been brought down, your face turned pale, and your bold words changed into speechless silence or dreadful cries, if God had only set you like this before his judgment seat and pleaded his own case with you, the case you have argued against so maliciously here! How easily he can at any time say to your guilty soul, “Come away, and live in that flesh no more until the resurrection,” and it cannot resist! One word from his mouth would take away the balance of your present life, and then all your faculties and powers would stand still. And if he says to you, “Live no longer, or live in hell,” you could not disobey.

But God has done none of this yet. He has patiently held back from you and mercifully upheld you. He has given you the very breath you breathed out against him, the mercies you sacrificed to your flesh, and the provisions you spent to satisfy your greedy throat. He gave you every minute of the time you wasted in idleness, drunkenness or worldliness. And does not all his patience and mercy show that he did not desire your damnation? Can the candle burn without the oil? Can your houses stand without the earth to bear them? You can no more live one hour without God’s support. And why did he support your life for so long, except to see when you would come to your senses about the folly of your ways, and turn back and live? Will anyone deliberately put weapons into his enemy’s hands to resist him, or hold a candle for a murderer who is killing his children, or for an idle servant who plays or sleeps meanwhile? Surely it is to see whether you will turn back at last and live that God has waited on you so long.

5. It is further proved by the suffering of his Son that God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked. Would he have ransomed them from death at so high a price? Would he have astonished angels and men by his condescension? Would God have dwelt in flesh, come in the form of a servant, and taken humanity into one person with the Godhead? And would Christ have lived a life of suffering and died a cursed death for sinners, if he would rather have taken pleasure in their death? Suppose you had seen him so busy preaching and healing them as you find him in Mark 3:21; or fasting so long, as in Matthew 4; or praying all night, as in Luke 6:12; or praying with drops of blood running from him instead of sweat, as in Luke 22:44; or suffering a cursed death on the cross and pouring out his soul as a sacrifice for our sins. Would you have thought these the signs of one who delighted in the death of the wicked?

And do not think to play it down by saying that it was only for his elect. For it was your sin, and the sin of all the world, that lay on our Redeemer; his sacrifice and satisfaction are sufficient for all, and its fruits are offered to one as well as another. But it is true that it was never his intention to pardon and save anyone who would not be converted by faith and repentance. If you had seen and heard him weeping and lamenting the state of disobedient, unrepentant people (Luke 19:41, 42), or complaining of their stubbornness, as in Matt. 23:37: “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how oft would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!”; or if you had seen and heard him on the cross praying for his persecutors, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do,” would you have suspected that he delighted in the death of the wicked, even of those who perish by their wilful unbelief? When God has so loved (not only loved, but so loved) the world as to give his only begotten Son, that whoever believes in him with an effectual faith should not perish but have everlasting life, I think he has proved by it, against the malice of men and devils, that he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but would rather they turned and lived.

6. Lastly, if all this still does not satisfy you, take his own word, since he knows his own mind best; or at least believe his oath. But this leads me on to the fourth doctrine.

Doctrine 4. The Lord has confirmed to us by his oath that he has no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but would rather they turned and lived; so that he may leave people no pretext for questioning its truth.

If you dare to question his word, I trust you dare not question his oath. Just as Christ has solemnly declared that the unregenerate and unconverted cannot enter the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 18:3; John 3:3), so God has sworn that his pleasure is not in their death but in their conversion and life. And as the Apostle says (Heb. 6:13, 16, 17, 18), because he can swear by no one greater than himself, he says, “As I live,” and so on. “For men verily swear by the greater, and an oath for confirmation is to them an end of all strife: wherein God, willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath, that by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation, who have fled for refuge, to lay hold on the hope set before us, which we have, as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast.” If anyone cannot reconcile this truth with the doctrine of predestination, or with the actual damnation of the wicked, that is his own ignorance; it leaves him no pretext for denying or questioning the truth of the point in hand. For this is confirmed by the oath of God, and so it must not be twisted to make it fit other points; rather, doubtful points must be made to fit it, and certain truths must be believed to agree with it, even though our shallow brains can hardly see how they agree.

USE.

If you are an unconverted sinner hearing these words, I now beg you to ponder the doctrines above a little, and think for a while about who it is that takes pleasure in your sin and damnation! It is certainly not God; he has sworn that for his part he takes no pleasure in it. And I know it is not pleasing him that you intend by it. You dare not say that you drink and swear, neglect holy duties and quench the promptings of the Spirit to please God. That would be like insulting the prince, breaking his laws and seeking his death, and saying you did it all to please him.

Who is it, then, that takes pleasure in your sin and death? No one who bears the image of God, for they must be of like mind with him. God knows it is little pleasure to your faithful teachers to see you serve your deadly enemy, madly gamble with your eternal state and deliberately run into the flames of hell. It is little pleasure to them to see in your souls (in their sad effects) such blindness, hard-heartedness, carelessness and presumption; such wilfulness in evil, and such unteachableness and stubbornness against the ways of life and peace. They know these are marks of death and of the wrath of God, and they know from the word of God what their end is likely to be. So it is no more pleasure to them than it is to a tender-hearted physician to see the plague spots break out on his patient. Alas! To foresee your everlasting torments and not know how to prevent them! To see how near you are to hell, and not be able to make you believe it and think about it! To see how easily, how certainly you might escape, if only we knew how to make you willing! How well placed you are for everlasting salvation, if only you would turn and do your best, and make it the care and business of your lives! But you will not do it. If our lives depended on it, we could not persuade you to it. We study day and night what to say to you that might convince and persuade you, and still it is not done. We lay the word of God before you and show you the very chapter and verse where it is written that you cannot be saved unless you are converted, and yet we leave most of you as we find you.—We hope you will believe the word of God, even if you do not believe us, and that you will heed it when we show you the plain Scripture for it; but we hope in vain and labour in vain as far as any saving change in your hearts goes. And do you think this is a pleasant thing for us? Many times in secret prayer we are forced to complain to God with sad hearts: “Alas, Lord, we have spoken to them in your name, but they pay little attention to us. We have told them what you told us to tell them about the danger of an unconverted state, but they do not believe us. We have told them that you have declared that ‘there is no peace to the wicked’ (Isa. 48:22 and 57:21), but even the worst of them will hardly believe that they are wicked. We have shown them your word, where you have said ‘that if they live after the flesh they shall die’ (Rom. 8:13); but they say they will believe in you, when they will not believe you; that they will trust in you, when they give no credit to your word; and when they hope that the threats of your words are false, they still call this hoping in God. And though we show them where you have said that when a wicked man dies all his hopes perish, still we cannot persuade them out of their deceitful hopes (Prov. 11:7).—We tell them what a low, unprofitable thing sin is; but they love it, and so will not leave it.—We tell them how dearly they buy this pleasure, and that they must pay for it in everlasting torment; and they bless themselves and will not believe it, but will do as most people do; and because God is merciful, they will not believe him, but will gamble with their souls, come what may. We tell them how ready the Lord is to receive them, and this only makes them delay their repentance and grow bolder in their sin.—Some of them say they intend to repent, but they are still the same; and some say they repent already, while they are still not converted from their sins. We exhort them, we plead with them, we offer them our help, but we cannot prevail with them. Those who were drunkards are drunkards still; those who were pleasure-loving, flesh-pleasing wretches are still the same; those who were worldlings are worldlings still; and those who were ignorant, proud and conceited are so still.—Few of them will see and confess their sin, and fewer will forsake it; they comfort themselves that all people are sinners, as if there were no difference between a converted sinner and an unconverted one. Some of them will not come near us when we are willing to instruct them, but think they know enough already and do not need our instruction. Some of them will give us a hearing and then do as they please. And most of them are like dead people who cannot feel, so that when we tell them of matters of everlasting consequence, we cannot get a word of it into their hearts. If we do not obey them and humour them by baptising the children of the most stubbornly wicked, giving them the Lord’s Supper, and doing everything they want, however much it is against the word of God, they will hate us and rail at us. But if we only beg them to confess and forsake their sins and save their souls, they will not do it.—We tell them that if they will only turn, we will deny them none of the ordinances of God, neither baptism for their children nor the Lord’s Supper for themselves; but they will not listen to us. They would have us disobey God and damn our own souls to please them, and yet they will not turn and save their own souls to please God.—They are wiser in their own eyes than all their teachers; they rage and are confident in their own way, and however much we would like to, we cannot change them. Lord, this is the state of our miserable neighbours, and we cannot help it. We see them about to drop into hell, and we cannot help it. We know that if they would sincerely turn they might be saved, but we cannot persuade them. If we begged it of them on our knees, we could not persuade them to it; if we begged it of them with tears, we could not persuade them; and what more can we do?”

These are the secret complaints and groans that many a poor minister is forced to make. And do you think he has any pleasure in this? Is it a pleasure to him to see you go on in sin and be unable to stop you? To see you so miserable and be unable even to make you aware of it? To see you merry when you cannot be sure of being an hour out of hell? To think what you must suffer for ever because you will not turn? And to think what an everlasting life of glory you deliberately despise and throw away? What sadder thing could you bring to their hearts? And how could you think of a way to grieve them more?

Who is it, then, that you please by your sin and death? It is none of your godly friends who understand. Alas, it grieves their souls to see your misery; they lament you many times when you give them little thanks for it, and when you have no heart to lament yourselves.

Who is it, then, that takes pleasure in your sin? No one but the three great enemies of God, whom you renounced at your baptism and have now treacherously turned to serve.

1. The devil certainly takes pleasure in your sin and death, for this is the very aim of all his temptations. For this he watches night and day. You could not think of a better way to please him than to go on in sin. How glad he is when he sees you going to the alehouse or to some other sin, and when he hears you curse or swear or rail! How glad he is when he hears you revile the minister who would draw you away from your sin and help to save you! These are his delight.

2. The wicked also delight in it, for it agrees with their nature.

3. But for all that, I know that it is not pleasing the devil that you intend, even when you please him. It is your own flesh, the greatest and most dangerous enemy, that you intend to please. It is the flesh that wants to be pampered, pleased with food and drink and clothing, pleased with your company, pleased with applause and reputation in the world, and pleased with sports and lusts and idleness. This is the pit that swallows everything. This is the very god you serve; for Scripture says of such people “that their bellies are their gods” (Phil. 3:18).

But I beg you to stop a little and consider the matter.

1. Question. Should your flesh be pleased before your Maker? Will you displease the Lord, and displease your teachers and your godly friends, all to please your brutish appetites or sensual desires? Is God not worthy to be the ruler of your flesh? If he is not to rule it, he will not save it; you cannot reasonably expect him to.

2. Question. Your flesh is pleased with your sin; but is your conscience pleased? Does it not grumble within you and tell you sometimes that all is not well, and that your case is not as safe as you make it out to be? And should not your soul and conscience be pleased before your perishable flesh?

3. Question. But is your flesh not preparing its own displeasure too? It loves the bait, but does it love the hook? It loves strong drink and sweet mouthfuls; it loves its ease, its sport and its merriment; it loves to be rich, well spoken of by people, and to be somebody in the world. But does it love the curse of God? Does it love to stand trembling before his judgment seat and be sentenced to everlasting fire? Does it love to be tormented with the devils for ever?—Take it all together; for there is no separating sin and hell except by faith and true conversion. If you will keep the one, you must have the other. If death and hell are pleasant to you, it is no wonder you go on in sin. But if they are not (as I am sure they are not), then, however pleasant sin may be, is it worth the loss of eternal life? Is a little drink, or food, or ease; is the good word of sinners; are the riches of this world to be valued above the joys of heaven? Or are they worth the sufferings of eternal fire?

These questions should be considered, before you go any further, by everyone who has the reason to consider them and who believes he has a soul to save or lose.

Well, the Lord swears here that he has no pleasure in your death, but would rather you turned and lived. If you still go on and die rather than turn, remember that it was not to please God that you did it; it was to please the world and to please yourselves. And if people will damn themselves to please themselves, and run into endless torments for the sake of delight, and have neither the sense, the heart nor the grace to listen to God or man who would reclaim them, what remedy is there? They must take what they get by it, and repent of it in another way when it is too late! Before I go any further in the application, I will come to the next doctrine, which gives me fuller grounds for it.

Doctrine 5. God is so earnest for the conversion of sinners that he doubles his commands and exhortations with urgency: “Turn ye, turn ye, why will ye die?”

This doctrine is the application of the one before, by way of exhortation, and I will treat it accordingly.

Is there an unconverted sinner hearing these urgent words of God? Is there a single man or woman in this congregation who is still a stranger to the renewing, sanctifying work of the Holy Spirit? It is a happy congregation if that is not true of most. Listen, then, to the voice of your Maker, and turn to him through Christ without delay. Do you want to know the will of God? This is his will: that you turn at once. Shall the living God send so earnest a message to his creatures, and shall they not obey? Listen, then, all you who live by the flesh: the Lord, who gave you your breath and being, has sent you a message from heaven, and this is his message: “Turn ye, turn ye, why will ye die?” Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear. Shall the voice of the eternal Majesty be neglected? If he only thunders terribly, you are afraid. Oh, but this word concerns your everlasting life or death. It is both a command and an exhortation. It is as if he said to you, “I charge you, by the allegiance you owe to me, your Creator and Redeemer, to renounce the flesh, the world and the devil, and turn to me so that you may live. I stoop to plead with you, as you love or fear the one who made you; as you love your own life, your everlasting life: turn and live. As you ever hope to escape eternal misery, turn, turn, for why will you die?” And is there a heart in man, in a rational creature, that can refuse such a message, such a command, such an exhortation as this even once? Oh, what a thing the human heart is, then!

Listen, then, all who love yourselves and care about your own salvation:—here is the most joyful message ever sent to human ears: “Turn ye, turn ye, for why will ye die?” You are not yet shut up in despair. Here is mercy offered to you; turn, and you shall have it. Oh, with what joyful hearts you should receive this news! I know this is not the first time you have heard it; but how have you heeded it, and how do you heed it now? Hear the word of the Lord, all you ignorant, careless sinners! Hear, all you worldlings and sensual flesh-pleasers; you gluttons and drunkards, whoremongers and swearers; you railers and backbiters, slanderers and liars: “Turn ye, turn ye, why will ye die?”

Hear, all you who are empty of the love of God, whose hearts are not towards him nor taken up with the hope of glory, but who think more of your earthly prosperity and pleasures than of the joys of heaven; all you who are religious only a little, on the side, and give God no more than your flesh can spare; who have not denied your carnal selves and given up all you have for Christ, in the judgment and settled resolve of your souls, but have some one thing in the world so dear to you that you could not part with it for Christ if he required it, and would rather risk his displeasure than give it up: “Turn ye, turn ye, why will ye die?”

If you never heard it or noticed it before, remember that you were told from the word of God today that if you will only turn, you may live; and if you will not turn, you will certainly die.

What will you do now, Sirs? What have you decided? Will you turn, or will you not? Do not waver any longer between two opinions. If the Lord is God, follow him; if your flesh is God, then go on serving it. If heaven is better than earth and fleshly pleasures, then come away and seek a better country, and “lay up your treasure where rust and moths do not corrupt, and thieves cannot break through and steal”; wake up at last with all your might to seek the kingdom that cannot be shaken (Heb. 12:28), spend your lives on a higher aim, and turn the stream of your cares and labours another way from before. But if earth is better than heaven, or will do more for you or last you longer, then keep it, make the best of it, and go on following it. Have you decided what to do? If you have not, I will set a few more moving considerations before you, to see whether reason will make you decide.

Consider first “what preparations mercy has made for your salvation,” and what a pity it is that anyone should be damned after all this. There was a time when the flaming sword was in the way, and the curse of God’s law would have kept you back however willing you had been to turn to God. There was a time when you and all the friends you have in the world could never have obtained pardon for your past sins, however much you had lamented them and reformed. But Christ has removed this obstacle by the ransom of his blood. There was a time when God was wholly unreconciled, not having received satisfaction for the violation of his law. But now he is so far satisfied and reconciled that he has made you a free act of pardon and a free deed of gift of Christ and life; he offers it to you and pleads with you to accept it, and it may be yours if you will. “For he was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, and hath committed to us the word of reconciliation” (2 Cor. 5:18, 19). Sinners, we too are commanded to deliver this message to all of you, as from the Lord: “Come, for all things are ready” (Luke 14:17). Are all things ready, and are you not ready? God is ready to welcome you and pardon all you have done against him, if you will only come. However long you have sinned, however wilfully you have sinned, he is ready to throw it all behind his back, if you will only come. Though you have been prodigals and run away from God and stayed away so long, he is ready even to meet you, embrace you in his arms and rejoice in your conversion, if you will only turn.—Even the earthly worldling and the swinish drunkard will find God ready to welcome them, if they will only come. Does this not turn your heart within you?—O sinner, if you have a heart of flesh and not of stone in you, I think this should melt it. Shall the infinite Majesty of Heaven actually wait for your return, and be ready to receive you, who have abused him and forgotten him so long? Shall he delight in your conversion, when he could at any moment glorify his justice in your damnation; and still it does not melt your heart within you, and you are still not ready to come in? Have you not as much reason to be ready to come as God has to invite you and welcome you?

But that is not all. Christ has done his part on the cross, and made such a way for you to the Father that for his sake you may be welcome if you will come. And are you still not ready?

A pardon is already expressly granted and offered to you in the gospel. And are you still not ready?

The ministers of the gospel are ready to help you and instruct you; they are ready to pray for you and to seal your pardon by administering the holy sacrament. And are you still not ready?

All around you who fear God are ready to rejoice in your conversion, to receive you into the communion of saints and to give you the right hand of fellowship, even if you had been someone put out of their company. They dare not do anything but forgive where God forgives, when it is made plain to them by your confession and amendment. They dare not even throw your former sins in your face, because they know that God will not reproach you with them. However scandalous you had been, if you would only be wholeheartedly converted and come in, they would not refuse you, whatever the world might say against it. And are all these ready to receive you, and are you still not ready to come in?

Indeed, heaven itself is ready. The Lord will receive you into the glory of his saints, vile brute that you have been; if you will only be cleansed, you may have a place before his throne; his angels will be ready to escort your soul to the place of joy, if you will only come in sincerely. And is God ready, the sacrifice of Christ ready, the promise ready and pardon ready?—Are ministers ready, the people of God ready, heaven itself ready and the angels ready, all only waiting for your conversion, and are you still not ready? What! Not ready to live, when you have been dead so long? Not ready to come to your right mind, as the prodigal is said to have come to himself (Luke 15:17), when you have been out of your mind so long? Not ready to be saved, when you are on the very point of being condemned?—Are you not ready to take hold of Christ, who would rescue you, when you are on the very point of drowning and sinking into damnation? Are you not ready to be saved from hell, when you are on the very point of being thrown into it beyond remedy? Alas, man! Do you know what you are doing? If you die unconverted, there is no doubt about your damnation, and you are not sure of living an hour; and are you still not ready to turn and come in? O miserable wretch! Have you not served the flesh and the devil long enough? Have you still not had enough of sin? Is it so good for you, or so profitable to you?—Do you know what it is, that you still want more of it? Have you had so many calls, so many mercies, so many blows and so many examples? Have you seen so many laid in the grave, and are you still not ready to let your sins go and come to Christ? What! After so many convictions and pangs of conscience, after so many intentions and promises, are you still not ready to turn and live?—Oh, that your eyes and your heart were opened to know how fair an offer is being made to you now, and what a joyful message we are sent with, to tell you to come, for all things are ready!

2. Consider also what calls you have to turn and live: how many, how loud, how earnest, how dreadful, and yet how encouraging and joyful.

For the chief one who invites you is God himself. He who commands heaven and earth commands you to turn, and to turn at once, without delay. He commands the sun to run its course and rise on you every morning; and though it is so glorious a creature, and many times bigger than the whole earth, it obeys him and does not fail by one minute of its appointed time. He commands all the planets and spheres of heaven, and they obey.—He commands the sea to ebb and flow, and the whole creation to keep its course, and all obey him. The angels of heaven obey his will when he sends them to minister to such feeble worms as we are on earth (Heb. 1:14).—And yet if he commands only a sinner to turn, he will not obey him. He thinks himself wiser than God; he quibbles and pleads the cause of sin, and will not obey. If the Lord Almighty says the word, the heavens and everything in them obey him; but if he calls just a drunkard out of an alehouse, he will not obey; or if he calls a worldly, fleshly sinner to deny himself, put the flesh to death and set his heart on a better inheritance, he will not obey him.

If you had any love in you, you would know the voice and say, “Oh, this is my Father’s call! How can I find it in my heart to disobey?” For “the sheep of Christ do know and hear his voice, and they follow him, and he giveth them eternal life” (John 10:4). If you had any spiritual life and feeling in you, you would at least say, “This call is the dreadful voice of God, and who dares disobey?”—For the prophet says (Amos 3:8), “The lion hath roared, who will not fear?” God is not a man, that you should toy and play with him. Remember what he said to Paul at his conversion: “It is hard for thee to kick against the pricks” (Acts 9:5). Will you still go and despise his word, resist his Spirit, and stop your ear against his call? Who will get the worst of this? Do you know whom you are disobeying and contending with, and what you are doing? It would be a far wiser and easier task for you to fight the thorns and kick them with your bare feet, or beat them with your bare hands, or put your head into the burning fire. “Be not deceived, God is not mocked” (Gal. 6:7). Whoever else is mocked, God will not be. You would do better to play with fire in your thatch than with the fire of his burning wrath; “for our God is a consuming fire” (Heb. 12:29). Oh, how unfit a match you are for God! “It is a fearful thing to fall into his hands” (Heb. 10:31); and so it is a fearful thing to contend with him or resist him. As you love your souls, take care what you do. What will you say if he begins to plead with you in wrath? What will you do once he takes you in hand? Will you not struggle against his judgment as you now struggle against his grace? The Lord says (Isa. 27:4, 5), “Fury is not in me;” that is, I do not delight to destroy you; I do it, as it were, unwillingly; but still, “Who would set the briars and thorns against me in battle? I would go through them, I would burn them together. Or let him take hold of my strength, that he may make peace with me; and he shall make peace with me.”—It is an unequal fight when briars and stubble make war with the fire.

And so you see who it is that calls you, which should move you to hear this call and turn. Consider also by what instruments, how often and how earnestly he does it.

1. Every page of the blessed book of God has a voice, as it were, and calls to you, Turn and live; turn, or you will die! How can you open it and read a page, or hear a chapter, and not see that God is telling you to turn?

2. It is the voice of every sermon you hear; for what else is the aim and drift of them all but to call, persuade and plead with you to turn?

3. It is the voice of many a prompting of the Spirit, which secretly repeats these words and urges you to turn.

4. Probably it is sometimes the voice of your own conscience. Are you not sometimes convinced that all is not well with you? And does your conscience not tell you that you must be a new person and take a new course, and often call you to turn back?

5. It is the voice of the gracious examples of the godly. When you see them live a heavenly life and flee from the sin that is your delight, this really calls on you to turn.

6. It is the voice of all the works of God. For they too are God’s books, which teach you this lesson by showing you his greatness, wisdom and goodness, and calling you to observe them and marvel at the Creator (Psa. 19:1, 2): “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament sheweth his handy work; day unto day uttereth speech, night unto night sheweth knowledge.”—Every time the sun rises on you, it really calls you to turn, as if it said, “Why do I travel round the world, except to declare to people the glory of their Maker and give them light to do his work? And do I still find you doing the work of sin and sleeping your life away in negligence? Awake, thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light” (Eph. 5:14). “The night is far spent, the day is at hand; it is now high time to awake out of sleep; let us therefore cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armour of light. Let us walk honestly as in the day, not in rioting and in drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying, but put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof” (Rom. 13:11, 12, 13, 14).—This text was the means of Augustine’s conversion.

7. It is the voice of every mercy you have. If you could only hear and understand them, they all cry out to you, Turn. Why does the earth carry you, except so that you may seek and serve the Lord? Why does it give you its fruits, except so that you may serve him? Why does the air give you breath, except so that you may serve him? Why do all the creatures serve you with their labours and their lives, except so that you may serve the Lord of them and of you? Why does he give you time and health and strength, except to serve him? Why do you have food and drink and clothes, except for his service? Do you have anything that you did not receive? And if you received it, it is only reasonable that you should consider from whom, and for what end and use, you received it. Did you never cry to him for help in your distress? And did you not understand then that it was your part to turn and serve him if he would deliver you? He has done his part, spared you longer still, and tried you another year and another; and still you do not turn? You know the parable of the barren fig tree (Luke 13:6, 7, 8, 9). When the Lord had said, “Cut it down, why cumbereth it the ground?” he was begged to try it one more year, and then, if it did not bear fruit, to cut it down. Christ himself makes the application there twice over (verses 3 and 5): “Except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.” How many years God has looked for the fruits of love and holiness from you and found none, and still has spared you! How many times, by your wilful ignorance, carelessness and disobedience, have you provoked justice to say, “Cut him down, why cumbereth he the ground?” And yet mercy has prevailed, and patience has held back the fatal blow to this day. If you had a man’s understanding within you, you would know that all this calls you to turn.—“Thinkest thou that thou shalt escape the judgment of God? Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness, and forbearance, and long-suffering, not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance? But, after thy hardness and impenitent heart, treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath, and revelation of the righteous judgment of God; who will render to every man according to his deeds” (Rom. 2:3, 4, 5, 6).

8. Moreover, it is the voice of every affliction, calling you to hurry and turn. Sickness and pain cry Turn; poverty, the loss of friends and every twig of the chastising rod cry Turn; and still you will not listen to the call? These have come close to you and made you feel; they have made you groan; and can they not make you turn?

9. The very make of your nature and your being itself call for your return. Why do you have reason, except to rule your flesh and serve your Lord? Why do you have an understanding soul, except to learn and know his will and do it? Why do you have a heart within you that can love and fear and desire, except so that you should fear him, love him and desire him?

10. Indeed, your own commitments, by promise to the Lord, call on you to turn and serve him. You bound yourself to him by a baptismal covenant and renounced the world, the flesh and the devil. You have confirmed this by professing Christianity, and renewed it at the sacraments and in times of affliction. And will you promise and vow and never perform it, and never turn to God?

Put all these together now, and see what the outcome should be. The holy Scripture calls on you to turn; the ministers of Christ call on you to turn; the Spirit cries Turn; your conscience cries Turn; the godly, by their persuasion and example, cry Turn; the whole world and all the creatures in it that are set before your mind cry Turn; the present patience of God cries Turn; all the mercies you receive cry Turn; the rod of God’s chastisement cries Turn; your reason and the make of your nature call for your turning, and so do all your promises to God. And still you have not resolved to turn?

11. Moreover, poor sinner, did you ever consider on what terms you stand all this while with the one who calls you to turn? You are his own, and owe him yourself and all you have; and may he not command his own? You are his servant absolutely, and should serve no other master. You stand at his mercy, and your life is in his hand; and he has decided to save you on no other terms. You have many malicious spiritual enemies who would be glad if God would only abandon you and leave you alone with them, to do as they like with you; how quickly they would deal with you in a different way! And you cannot be delivered from them except by turning to God. You have already fallen under his wrath by your sin, and you do not know how much longer his patience will wait. Perhaps this is the last year; perhaps the last day. His sword is at your very heart while the word is in your ear; and if you do not turn, you are a dead and ruined man. If only your eyes were open to see where you stand, on the very brink of hell, and to see how many thousands are there already who did not turn, you would see that it is time to look around you.

Well, Sirs, look inside now and tell me: how are your hearts affected by these offers of the Lord? You hear his mind: he does not delight in your death; he calls to you, Turn, turn. It is a fearful sign if all this does not move you, or moves you only halfway; and much more so if it makes you more careless in your misery because you hear of the mercifulness of God. How the medicine works will partly tell us whether there is any hope of a cure. Oh, what glad news it would be to those who are now in hell if only they had such a message from God! What a joyful word it would be to hear this: Turn and live.—Indeed, what a welcome word it would be to you yourself, when you had felt the wrath of God for only an hour! Or if, after a thousand or ten thousand years of torment, you could only hear such a word from God, Turn and live! And will you neglect it now, and let us go back without having done our errand?

See, sinners, we are sent here as the messengers of the Lord to set life and death before you. What do you say? Which of them will you choose? Christ stands beside you, as it were, with heaven in one hand and hell in the other, and offers you your choice; which will you choose?—“The voice of the Lord makes the rocks to tremble” (Psa. 26). And is it nothing to hear him threaten you, if you will not turn? Do you not understand and feel this voice, “Turn ye, turn ye, why will ye die?”—It is the voice of love, of infinite love, of your best and kindest friend, as you could easily see from what it urges; and can you still neglect it? It is the voice of pity and compassion. The Lord sees where you are going better than you do, and that makes him call after you, “Turn, turn.” He sees what will become of you if you do not turn. He thinks to himself, “Ah, this poor sinner will throw himself into endless torments if he does not turn; I must in justice deal with him according to my righteous law;” and so he calls after you, Turn, turn, O sinner! If you knew even a thousandth part as well as God does of the danger that is near you and the misery you are running into, we would have no more need to call after you to turn.

Moreover, this voice that calls to you is the same voice that has already prevailed with thousands and called to heaven all who are there now; and they would not now, for a thousand worlds, have made light of it and not turned to God. What do they possess now, who turned at God’s call? Now they see that it really was the voice of love, which meant them no harm, only their salvation. And if you will obey the same call, you will come to the same happiness. There are millions who must lament for ever that they did not turn; but there is not one soul in heaven who is sorry to have been converted.

Well, Sirs, have you decided yet, or not? Do I need to say any more to you? What will you do? Will you turn, or not? Speak, man, in your heart to God, even if you do not speak out to me. Speak, in case he takes your silence for refusal. Speak quickly, in case he never makes you such an offer again. Speak with determination and not with wavering, for he will have no half-hearted followers. Say in your heart now, without any more delay, even before you move from here: “By the grace of God I am resolved to turn at once. And because I know my own inadequacy, I am resolved to wait on God for his grace, to follow him in his ways, to leave my former ways and companions, and to give myself up to the guidance of the Lord.”

You are not shut up in the darkness of heathenism, nor in the despair of the damned.—Life is before you, and you may have it on reasonable terms if you will; indeed, free of cost, if you will accept it. The way of God lies plain before you; the church is open to you; you may have Christ and pardon and holiness, if you will. What do you say? Will you, or will you not? If you say no, or say nothing and still go on, God is witness, this congregation is witness, and your own consciences are witnesses, how fair an offer you had today. Remember that you could have had Christ, and would not. Remember, when you have lost it, that you could have had eternal life as well as others, and would not; and all because you would not turn.

fields.title: Sermon III
fields.body_html:
Ezek. 33:11.

Say to them, As I live, saith the Lord God, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live. Turn ye, turn ye, from your evil ways, for, why will ye die, O house of Israel?

IT has been explained and proved that God takes pleasure in people’s conversion and salvation, but not in their death or damnation. He would rather they turned and lived than went on and died.—So that he may leave people no pretext for doubting it, the Lord has confirmed it to us by his oath. And further, God is so earnest for the conversion of sinners that he doubles his commands and exhortations with urgency: Turn ye, turn ye.

Having already illustrated and applied each of these points, let us come to the next doctrine and hear your reasons.

Doctrine 6. The Lord stoops to reason the case with unconverted sinners, and to ask them why they will die.

It is a strange debate, both in its question and in those who take part in it.

1. The question put up for debate is, “Why will wicked people damn themselves?” or, “Why will they rather die than turn?” Do they have any sufficient reason for doing so?

2. Those in the debate are God and man: the most holy God, and wicked, unconverted sinners.

Is it not a strange thing, which God seems to assume here, that anyone should be willing to die and be damned? And that this should be the case of the wicked, that is, of the greater part of the world? But you will say, This cannot be; for nature desires its own preservation and happiness, and the wicked are more selfish than others, not less; so how can anyone be willing to be damned?—I answer:

1. It is a certain truth that no one can will any evil as evil, but only as it has some appearance of good; much less can anyone be willing to be tormented eternally. No one desires misery as such.

2. Yet for all that, what God teaches us here is most true: the reason the wicked die and are damned is that they will die and be damned. And this is true in several respects.

1.
