They will go the way that leads to hell, though God and man tell them where it goes and where it ends, and though God has declared so often in his word that if they keep on in that way they will be condemned, and that they will not be saved unless they turn (Isa. 48:22 and 57:21): “There is no peace, saith the Lord, unto the wicked.” Isa. 59:8: “The way of peace they know not; there is no judgment in their goings; they have made them crooked paths; whosoever goeth therein shall not know peace.” They have the word and the oath of the living God for it that if they will not turn, they will not enter his rest.—And yet wicked they are, and wicked they will be, whatever God and man say. Fleshly they are, and fleshly they will be; worldlings they are, and worldlings they will be; though God has told them that “the love of the world is enmity to God; and that if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him” (James 4:4; 1 John 2:15). So these people are, as a consequence, willing to be damned, though not directly. They are willing to walk the road to hell and love the certain cause of their torment, though they are not willing for hell itself and do not love the pain they must endure.

Is this not the truth of your case, sinners? You would not want to burn in hell; but you will light the fire by your sins and throw yourselves into it. You would not want to be tormented with devils for ever; but you will do what will certainly bring it about, in spite of all that can be said against it. It is just as if you said, “I will drink this poison, but I will not die. I will throw myself headlong from the top of a steeple, but I will not kill myself.—I will push this knife into my heart, but I will not take my life. I will put this fire into the thatch of my house, but I will not burn it down.”—It is just the same with wicked people. They will be wicked, and they will live by the flesh and the world, and yet they would not be damned. But do you not know that the means lead to the end, and that God has determined by his righteous law that you must repent or perish? Someone who will take poison might as well say plainly, “I will kill myself;” for it will come to no better in the end. Perhaps he loved it for the sweetness of the sugar mixed with it, and would not be persuaded that it was poison, but thought he could take it and do well enough; but his notions and confidence will not save his life. So if you will be drunkards, or fornicators, or worldlings, or live by the flesh, you might as well say plainly, “We will be damned;” for so you will be, unless you turn. Would you not rebuke the folly of a thief or murderer who said, “I will steal and kill, but I will not be hanged,” when he knows that if he does the one, the judge will in justice see that the other is done? If he says, “I will steal and murder,” he might as well say plainly, “I will be hanged.” So if you will go on in a carnal life, you might as well say plainly, “We will go to hell.”

2. Moreover, the wicked will not use the means without which there is no hope of their salvation. Someone who will not eat might as well say plainly that he will not live, unless he can tell how to live without food. Someone who will not make his journey might as well say plainly that he will not arrive. Someone who falls into the water and will not come out, nor let anyone help him out, might as well say plainly that he will be drowned. So if you are carnal and ungodly and will not be converted, nor use the means by which you should be converted, but think it more fuss than is needed, you might as well say plainly that you will be damned. For if you have found a way to be saved without conversion, you have done what was never done before.

3. Indeed, that is not all. The wicked are unwilling even to share in salvation itself. Though they may desire something they call heaven, they do not desire heaven itself, considered in the true nature of its happiness; their hearts are entirely against it. Heaven is a state of perfect holiness and of continual love and praise to God, and the wicked have no heart for this. They have no interest in the imperfect love and praise and holiness that can be reached here, much less in what is so much greater. The joys of heaven are of so pure and spiritual a nature that the heart of the wicked cannot desire them.

So by now you may see on what grounds God assumes that the wicked are willing for their own destruction. They will rather risk certain misery than be converted; and then, to quiet themselves in their sins, they make themselves believe that they will escape anyway.

2. And just as this question is a matter for wonder (that people should be such enemies to themselves as deliberately to throw away their souls), so are those in the debate. That God should stoop so low as to plead the case with man like this; and that people should be so strangely blind and stubborn as to need all this in so plain a case; and even resist all this, when their own salvation depends on the outcome!

It is no wonder they will not listen to us, who are men, when they will not listen to the Lord himself. As God said (Ezek. 3:7) when he sent the prophet to the Israelites, “The house of Israel will not hearken unto thee; for they will not hearken unto me: for all the house of Israel are impudent and hard-hearted.” It is no wonder if they can argue against a minister or a godly neighbour, when they will argue against the Lord himself, even against the plainest passages of his word, and think they have reason on their side. When they weary the Lord with their words, they say, “Wherein have we wearied him?” (Mal. 2:17). The priests who despised his name dared to ask, “Wherein have we despised thy name?” And when they polluted his altar and made the temple of the Lord contemptible, they dared to say, “Wherein have we polluted thee?” (Mal. 1:6, 7). But “Woe unto him, saith the Lord, that striveth with his Maker: Let the potsherd strive with the potsherds of the earth: Shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, What makest thou?” (Isa. 45:9).

Question. But why does God reason the case with man?

Answer. 1. Because man is a rational creature and is to be dealt with accordingly, persuaded and won over by reason. God gave people reason so that they might use it for him. One would think a rational creature would not go against the clearest and greatest reason in the world when it is set before him.

2. At least people will see that God required nothing unreasonable of them, but that in whatever he forbids them he has all the right reason in the world on his side; and that they had good reason to obey him, and none to disobey. And so even the damned will be forced to justify God and admit that it was only reasonable that they should have turned to him; and they will be forced to condemn themselves and admit that they had little reason to throw themselves away by neglecting his grace in the day of their visitation.

USE.

Dig out your best and strongest reasons, sinners, if you mean to make your case good.—You see now whom you have to deal with.—What do you say, unconverted, sensual sinner? Dare you venture on a debate with God? Are you able to refute him? Are you ready to enter the lists? God asks you, Why will you die? Are you equipped with a sufficient answer? Will you undertake to prove that God is mistaken and that you are right? Oh, what an undertaking that is!—Either he or you must be mistaken, when he is for your conversion and you are against it. He calls on you to turn, and you will not. He tells you to do it at once, today, while it is called today, and you delay and think there will be time enough later.—He says it must be a total change, that you must be holy, new creatures, born again; and you think less will do, and that it is enough to patch up the old self without becoming new. Who is right now, God or you? God calls on you to turn and live a holy life, and you will not; your disobedient lives show that you will not. If you will, why do you not? Why have you not done it all this while? And why do you not set about it even now? Your wills have command of your lives. We can certainly conclude that you are unwilling to turn when you do not turn. And why will you not? Can you give any reason for it that deserves to be called a reason?

I, who am only a worm, your fellow creature, of shallow capacity, dare to challenge the wisest of you to reason the case with me while I plead my Maker’s cause. And I need not be discouraged, since I know I am pleading only the cause God pleads, and contending for the one who will have the best of it in the end. If I had only these two general grounds against you, I would be sure you have no good reason on your side.

1. I am sure that nothing can be a good reason that is against the God of truth and reason. Nothing that contradicts the sun can be light. There is no knowledge in any creature except what it has from God, and so no one can be wiser than God. It would be fatal presumption for the highest angel to compare himself with his Creator. What is it, then, for a lump of dirt, an ignorant fool who does not know himself or his own soul, who knows little of the things he sees, and is more ignorant than many of his neighbours, to set himself against the wisdom of the Lord? It is one of the plainest revelations of the horrible wickedness of carnal people, and the utter madness of those who sin, that so feeble a mole dares to contradict his Maker and call the word of God into question. Indeed, people in our parishes who are so ignorant that they cannot give us a reasonable answer about the very first principles of religion are still so wise in their own eyes that they dare to question the plainest truths of God, even contradict them and quibble against them, when they can hardly talk sense, and will believe them no further than they agree with their own foolish wisdom.

2. And just as I know that God must be in the right, so I know that the thing he pleads against is so obviously and grossly wrong that no one can have a reason for it. Is it possible for anyone to have a reason to break his master’s laws? A reason to dishonour the Lord of glory? A reason to abuse the Lord who bought him? Is it possible for anyone to have a good reason to damn his own immortal soul?—Notice the Lord’s question: “Turn ye, turn ye, why will ye die?” Is eternal death something to be desired? Are you in love with hell? What reason do you have to perish wilfully? If you think you have a reason to sin, should you not remember that “the wages of sin is death” (Rom. 6:23), and consider whether you have any reason to ruin yourselves, body and soul, for ever?—You should ask not only whether you love the adder, but whether you love its sting.—For a person to throw away his everlasting happiness and to sin against God is such a thing that no good reason can be given for it; the more anyone pleads for it, the madder he shows himself to be. If you were offered a lordship or a kingdom for every sin you commit, it would be madness, not reason, to accept. If by every sin you could obtain the highest thing on earth that the flesh desires, it would be of no value worth considering to persuade you, by reason, to commit it. If it were to please your greatest or dearest friends, or to obey the greatest prince on earth, or to save your lives, or to escape the greatest earthly misery, none of these would be worth considering, by reason, to draw a person into committing one sin. If it were a right hand or a right eye that would hinder your salvation, the most profitable course is to throw it away rather than go to hell to save it; for there is no saving a part when you lose the whole. The matters of eternity are so exceedingly great that nothing in this world deserves even to be mentioned in comparison with them; nor can any earthly thing, even life, or crowns, or kingdoms, be a reasonable excuse for neglecting matters of such high and everlasting consequence. A person can have no reason to go against his ultimate end. Heaven is such a thing that if you lose it, nothing can make up the lack or the loss; and hell is such a thing that if you suffer it, nothing can remove your misery or give you ease and comfort. So nothing can be a consideration of enough value to excuse you for neglecting your own salvation; for, our Saviour says, “What shall it profit a man if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?” (Mark 8:36).

O Sirs, if only you knew what matters these are that we are speaking to you about now! The saints in heaven think very differently about these things. If the devil could come to those who live in the sight and love of God and offer them a cup of ale, or a whore, or merry company, or sport, to entice them away from God and glory, tell me, how do you think they would receive the proposal? Or if he offered to make them kings of the earth, do you think this would entice them down from heaven? Oh, with what hatred and holy scorn they would disdain and reject the proposal! And why should you not do the same, when heaven is opened to your faith, if only you had faith to see it? There is not one soul in hell who does not know by now that it was a mad exchange to let heaven go for fleshly pleasure, and that a little merriment, or pleasure, or worldly riches, or honour, or the goodwill or good word of people, will not quench hell fire, or make anyone who loses his soul come out ahead. Oh, if you had heard what I believe, if you had seen what I believe, and that on the credit of the word of God, you would say there can be no reason that justifies anyone in damning his soul. You would not dare to sleep quietly another night until you had resolved to turn and live.

If you saw someone hold his hand in the fire until it burned off, you would marvel at it; but this is something a person may have a reason for, as Bishop Cranmer had when he burned off his hand for signing in favour of Popery. If you see someone cut off a leg or an arm, it is a sad sight; but this is something a person may have good reason for, as many do to save their lives. If you see someone give his body to be burned to ashes and tormented on the rack, and refuse deliverance when it is offered, that is hard for flesh and blood; but a person may have good reason for this, as you may see in Heb. 11:33, 34, 35, 36, and as many hundreds of martyrs have done. But for someone to forsake the Lord who made him and run into the fire of hell, when he is told of it and begged to turn so that he may be saved: this is something for which there can be no reason in the world, no real reason, to justify or excuse it. For heaven will repay the loss of anything we may lose to get it; but nothing can repay the loss of heaven.

I beg you now, let this word come closer to your hearts. Since you are convinced that you have no reason to destroy yourselves, tell me what reason you have for refusing to turn and live for God. What reason does the most thorough worldling, or drunkard, or ignorant, careless sinner among you have for not being as holy as anyone you know, and as careful for your soul as anyone else? Will hell not be as hot for you as for others? Should your own souls not be as dear to you as theirs are to them? Does God not have as much authority over you? Why, then, will you not become a sanctified people as well as they?

O Sirs, when God brings the matter down to the very first principles of nature, and shows that you have no more reason to be ungodly than you have to damn your own souls, if you still will not understand and turn, it seems you are in a desperate state. Now, either you have a reason for what you do, or you do not. If not, will you go against reason itself? Will you do what you have no reasons for? But if you think you do, bring them out and make the best of your case. Reason the case a little with me, your fellow creature, which is far easier than reasoning the case with God. Tell me, man, here before the Lord, as if you were to die this hour: why should you not resolve to turn today, before you move from the place where you are standing? What reason do you have to refuse or delay? Do you have any reason for it that satisfies your own conscience? Or any that you dare to own and plead at the judgment seat of God? If you have, let us hear them; bring them out and make them good. But alas! What poor stuff, what nonsense instead of reasons, we hear every day from ungodly people! If it were not necessary, I would be ashamed to name them.

1. One says, “If no one will be saved but such converted and sanctified people as you talk about, then heaven will be empty; God help a great many!”

Answer. What! It seems you think either that God does not know, or that he is not to be believed! Do not measure everything by yourselves. God has thousands and millions of sanctified ones; but they are still few compared with the world, as Christ himself has told us (Matt. 7:13, 14; Luke 12:32). It would suit you better to make the use of this truth that Christ teaches you: “Strive to enter in at the strait gate; for strait is the gate, and narrow is the way that leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it; but wide is the gate and broad is the way, that leads to destruction, and many there be that go in thereat” (Luke 13:22, 23, 24).—“Fear not, little flock (says Christ to his sanctified ones), for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12:32).

Objection. 2. I am sure that if people like me go to hell, we will have plenty of company.

Answer. And will that be any relief or comfort to you? Or do you think you cannot have company enough in heaven? Will you be ruined for the sake of company? Or will you refuse to believe that God will carry out his threats because so many are guilty? These are all foolish, unreasonable notions.

Objection. 3. But all people are sinners, even the best of you.

Answer. But not all are unconverted sinners. The godly do not live in gross sins; and their very weaknesses are their grief and burden, which they long and pray and strive every day to be rid of. Sin does not have dominion over them.

Objection. 4. I do not see that those who profess religion are any better than other people; they will cheat and oppress, and are as greedy as anyone.

Answer. Whatever hypocrites are, it is not so with those who are sanctified. God has thousands and tens of thousands who are different, though the malicious world accuses them of what it can never prove, and of what never entered their hearts. And it usually charges them with sins of the heart, which no one but God can see, because it can charge them with no such wickedness in their lives as it is guilty of itself.

Objection. 5. But I am no whoremonger, nor drunkard, nor oppressor; so why do you call me to be converted?

Answer. As if you were not born of the flesh, and had not lived by the flesh, as well as others! Is it not as great a sin as any of these for someone to have an earthly mind, to love the world above God, and to have an unbelieving, unhumbled heart? Indeed, let me tell you more: many people who avoid disgraceful sins are as firmly glued to the world, as much slaves to the flesh, as much strangers to God and as averse to heaven in their more respectable way of life as others are in their more shameful and notorious sins.

Objection. 6. But I mean nobody any harm, and do no harm; so why should God condemn me?

Answer. Is it no harm to neglect the Lord who made you and the work for which you came into the world, to prefer the creature to the Creator, and to neglect the grace that is offered to you every day? It is the depth of your sinfulness that you do not feel it; the dead do not feel that they are dead. If you were once made alive, you would see more wrong in yourself, and marvel at yourself for making so light of it.

Objection. 7. I think you would drive people mad on the pretext of converting them. It is enough to rack the brains of sinful people to brood so much on matters too high for them.

Answer. 1. Can you be madder than you are already? Or at least, can there be a more dangerous madness than neglecting your everlasting welfare and deliberately ruining yourselves?

2. A person is never in his right mind until he is converted. He never knows God, nor sin, nor Christ, nor the world, nor himself, nor what his business on earth is, so as to set about it, until he is converted.—Scripture says “that the wicked are unreasonable men” (2 Thess. 3:2), and “that the wisdom of the world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. 1:20; Luke 15:17). It is said of the prodigal that “when he came to himself” he resolved to return.—It is a wise world indeed when people will disobey God and run to hell for fear of losing their wits.

3. What is there in the work Christ calls you to that should drive anyone out of his wits? Is it loving God, calling on him, thinking with comfort of the glory to come, forsaking our sins, loving one another and delighting ourselves in the service of God? Are these the kind of things that should drive people mad?

4. And when you say that these matters are too high for us, you accuse God himself for making this our work, giving us his word, and commanding all who want to be blessed to meditate on it day and night. Are the things we are made for and live for too high for us to have anything to do with? This is plainly to take away our humanity and make brutes of us, as if we were like those who must have nothing to do with anything higher than what belongs to flesh and earth. If heaven is too high for you to think about and prepare for, it will be too high for you ever to possess.

5. If God sometimes allows some weak-minded people to become distracted by thinking of eternal things, it is because they misunderstand them and run on without a guide. And of the two, I would rather be in such a person’s condition than in that of the mad, unconverted world, which takes its distraction for wisdom.

Objection. 8. I do not think God cares so much about what people think or say or do as to make such a big thing of it.

Answer. It seems, then, that you take the word of God to be false; and then what will you believe? But your own reason could teach you better, even if you do not believe the Scriptures. For you see that God does not think so little of us; he is pleased to make us, and still preserves us, upholds us daily and provides for us. And will any wise person make an intricate mechanism for nothing? Will you make or buy a clock or watch, look at it every day, and not care whether it keeps true time or not? Surely, if you do not believe that a particular eye of Providence watches your hearts and lives, you cannot believe in or expect any particular Providence to watch your needs and troubles and relieve you. And if God had cared as little for you as you imagine, you would never have lived until now. A hundred diseases would have competed to destroy you first; indeed, the devils would have haunted you and carried you off alive, as the great fish devour the smaller ones and as ravenous birds and beasts devour others. You cannot think that God made man for no end or use; and if he made him for any end, it was surely for himself. And can you think he does not care whether his ends are achieved, and whether we do the work we are made for?

Indeed, by this atheistic objection you make God to have made and upheld the whole world in vain. For what are all the other, lower creatures for, if not for man? What does the earth do but carry us and feed us? The beasts serve us with their labours and their lives, and so on with the rest. And has God made so glorious a dwelling, set man to live in it, and made everything his servant, and does he now look for nothing from him, nor care how he thinks or speaks or lives? This is most unreasonable.

Objection. 9. It was a better world when people did not make such a fuss about religion.

Answer. 1. It has always been the custom to praise times past. The world you speak of used to say it was a better world in their forefathers’ days, and their forefathers said the same of theirs. This is just an old habit, because we all feel the evils of our own times, but do not see those that came before us.

2. Perhaps you speak as you think. Worldlings think the world is at its best when it suits their minds, and when they have the most merriment and worldly pleasure. And I do not doubt that the devil would say, as you do, that it was a better world then, for then he had more service and less disturbance. But the world is at its best when God is most loved, honoured and obeyed. And how else will you know when the world is good or bad, if not by this?

Objection. 10. There are so many ways and religions that we do not know which to belong to, and so we will stay just as we are.

Answer. Because there are many, will you belong to the way you can be sure is wrong? No one is further off the way than worldly, fleshly, unconverted sinners; for they err not just in this or that opinion, but in the very aim and drift of their lives. If you were making a journey on which your life depended, would you stop or turn back because you came to some crossroads, or because you saw some travellers take the bridleway and some the footpath, and some perhaps break through the hedge, and some even miss the way? Or would you not rather take all the more care to ask the way? If you had some servants who did not know how to do your work properly, and some who were unfaithful, would you take it kindly if any of the rest were idle and did you no service because they saw their companions were so bad?

Objection. 11. I do not see that things go any better for those who are so godly than for other people; they are as poor and in as much trouble as others.

Answer. And perhaps in much more, when God sees fit. They do not take earthly prosperity as their wages. They have laid up their treasure and hopes in another world, or else they are not real Christians. The less they have, the more is still to come, and they are content to wait until then.

Objection. 12. When you have said all you can, I am resolved to hope for the best, trust in God, do as well as I can, and not make such a fuss.

Answer. 1. Is that doing as well as you can, when you will not turn to God and your heart is against his holy and diligent service? It is as well as you will, certainly; but that is your misery.

2. My desire is that you should hope and trust in God. But what is it you would hope for? Is it to be saved if you turn and are sanctified? For this you have God’s promise, so hope for it, and do not hold back. But if you hope to be saved without conversion and a holy life, this is not hoping in God but in Satan or in yourselves; for God has given you no such promise, but has told you the opposite. It is Satan and self-love that made you such promises and raised such hopes in you.—Well, if these and others like them are all you have to say against conversion and a holy life, your all is nothing, and worse than nothing. And if these and others like them seem reasons enough to persuade you to forsake God and throw yourselves into hell, the Lord deliver you from such reasons, from such blind understandings, and from such senseless, hardened hearts. Dare you stand by one of these reasons at the judgment seat of God? Do you think it will serve your purpose then to say, “Lord, I did not turn because I had so much to do in the world; or because I did not like the lives of some who professed religion; or because I saw people of so many opinions”?—Oh, how easily the light of that day will put such reasoning to shame! Did you have the world to look after? Let the world you served pay you your wages now, and save you if it can. Did you not have a better world to look after first? And were you not commanded to “seek first God’s kingdom and righteousness,” and promised “that other things should be added to you”? (Matt. 6:33). And were you not told “that godliness was profitable unto all things, having the promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come”? (1 Tim. 4:8). Did the sins of those who professed religion hold you back? You should rather have been all the more watchful, learned from their falls to beware, and been more careful, not more careless. It was Scripture, not their lives, that was your rule. Did the many opinions in this world hold you back? Scripture, which was your rule, taught you only one way, and that was the right way. If you had followed it, even in as much of it as was plain and easy, you would never have gone wrong. Will answers like these not silence you? If these will not, God has answers that will, as when he asks the man (Matt. 22:12), “Friend, how camest thou in hither, not having a wedding garment?” That is, what are you doing in my church among professing Christians without a holy heart and life? What answer did he give? The text says he was speechless; he had nothing to say. The plainness of the case and the Majesty of God will easily stop the mouths of the most confident of you then, though you will not be put down by anything we can say to you now, but will defend your case, however bad it is. I already know that no reason you can give me now will do you any good at the last, when your case must be laid open before the Lord and all the world. Indeed, I hardly think your own consciences are well satisfied with your reasons. For if they are, it seems you have not even intended to repent. But if you intend to repent, it seems you do not put much confidence in the reasons you bring against it. What do you say, unconverted sinners? Have you any good reasons to give why you should not turn, and turn at once, with all your hearts? Or will you go to hell in spite of reason itself? Think about what you are doing in time, for it will soon be too late to think about it.—Can you find any fault with God, or his work, or his wages? Is he a bad master? Is the devil, whom you serve, a better one? Or is the flesh a better one? Is there any harm in a holy life? Is a life of worldliness and ungodliness better? Do you think, in your consciences, that it would do you any harm to be converted and live a holy life? What harm could it do you? Is it harm to you to have the Spirit of Christ within you, and a cleansed, purified heart? If it is bad to be holy, why does God say, “Be ye holy, for I am holy”? (1 Pet. 1:15, 16; Lev. 20:7). Is it evil to be like God? Is it not said “that God made man in his own image”? This holiness is his image. Adam lost it, and Christ by his word and Spirit would restore it to you, as he does to all he will save. Why were you baptised into the Holy Spirit, and why do you have your children baptised into the Holy Spirit as your sanctifier, if you will not be sanctified by him but think it hard to be sanctified? Tell me truly, as before the Lord: although you are unwilling to live a holy life, would you not rather die in the condition of those who do than of others? If you were to die today, would you not rather die in the condition of a converted person than of an unconverted one? Of a holy and heavenly person than of a carnal, earthly one? And would you not say with Balaam (Num. 23:10), “Let me die the death of the righteous, and let my last end be like his”? And why will you not now be of the mind you will be of then? Sooner or later you must come to this: either to be converted, or to wish you had been, when it is too late. But what is it you are afraid of losing if you turn? Is it your friends? You will only exchange them. God will be your friend, and Christ and the Spirit will be your friends, and every Christian will be your friend. You will gain one friend who will be of more use to you than all the friends in the world could have been. The friends you lose would only have enticed you to hell, but could not have rescued you. But the friend you gain will save you from hell and bring you to his own eternal rest.

Is it your pleasure you are afraid of losing? You think you will never have a merry day again once you are converted. Alas, that you should think it a greater pleasure to live in foolish sports and merriment and to please your flesh than to live in believing thoughts of glory, in the love of God, and in righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit, which is what the state of grace consists in! (Rom. 14:17). If it would be a greater pleasure for you to think of your lands and inheritance (if you owned the whole county) than it is for a child to play for pins, why should it not be a greater joy to you to think of the kingdom of heaven being yours than of all the riches and pleasures of the world? Just as it is only foolish childishness that makes children delight so much in toys that they would not give them up for all your land, so it is only foolish worldliness, fleshliness and wickedness that make you delight so much in your houses and lands, food and drink, ease and honour that you would not part with them for heavenly delights. But what will you do for pleasure when these are gone? Do you not think of that? When your pleasures end in horror and go out like a stinking candle-end, the pleasures of the saints are then at their best. I myself have had only a little taste of heavenly pleasures, in looking forward to the blessed approaching day and in the present assurance of the love of God in Christ; but I have drunk too deeply of earthly pleasures, so you can see that if I am biased, it is on your side. And yet I must declare, from that little experience, that there is no comparison.—There is more joy to be had in a single day in the state of holiness (if the sun of life shines clearly on us) than in a whole life of sinful pleasures. I had “rather be a door-keeper in the house of God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness” (Psa. 84:10). “A day in his courts is better than a thousand anywhere else” (Psa. 84:10). The merriment of the wicked is like the laughter of a madman who does not know his own misery; and so Solomon says of such laughter, “It is mad: and of mirth, What doeth it?” (Eccles. 2:2), and in Eccles. 7:2, 3, 4, 5, 6: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting; for that is the end of all men, and the living will lay it to his heart. Sorrow is better than laughter; for by the sadness of the countenance the heart is made better. The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning; but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth. It is better to hear the rebuke of the wise, than to hear the song of fools; for as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool.” All the pleasure of fleshly things is like the scratching of a man who has the itch: it is his disease that makes him want it, and a wise man would rather be without the pleasure than be troubled with the itch. Your loudest laughter is like that of a man being tickled: he laughs when he has no reason for joy. Judge, as rational people, whether this is the part of a wise person. It is only your carnal, unsanctified nature that makes a holy life seem burdensome to you and a course of sensuality seem more delightful. If you will only turn, the Holy Spirit will give you another nature and inclination, and then it will be more pleasant to you to be rid of your sin than it is now to keep it. And then you will say that you did not know what a comfortable life was until now, and that it was never well with you until God and holiness were your delight.

Question. But how does it come about that people are so unreasonable in the matter of salvation? They have sense enough in other matters. What makes them so unwilling to be converted that so many words are needed in so plain a case, and none of it will do, but most people will live and die unconverted?

Answer. To name them only in a few words, the causes are these:

1. People are naturally in love with the earth and the flesh, and their nature has a hostility to God and godliness, as the nature of a serpent has towards a human being. And when everything we can say goes against a settled inclination of their nature, it is no wonder if it achieves little.

2. They are in darkness, and do not know the very things they hear. They are like someone born blind who hears high praise of the light: what good will hearing do unless he sees it? They do not know what God is, nor the power of the cross of Christ, nor what the Spirit of holiness is, nor what it is to live in love by faith. They do not know the certainty, fitness and excellence of the heavenly inheritance. They do not know what conversion and a holy mind and life are, even when they hear about them. They are in a fog of ignorance. They are lost and bewildered in sin, like someone who has lost his way at night and does not know where he is or how to find himself again until the daylight rescues him.

3. They are wilfully confident that they need no conversion, only some partial improvement; that they are already on the way to heaven; and that they are converted when they are not. And if you meet someone who is quite off his way, you may call on him to turn back for as long as you like if he will not believe you that he is off the way.

4. They have become slaves to their flesh, and are drowned in the world in making provision for it. Their lusts, passions and appetites have distracted them and got such a hold over them that they do not know how to deny them or how to think about anything else. So the drunkard says, “I love a cup of good drink, and I cannot give it up.” The glutton says, “I love good food, and I cannot give it up.” The fornicator says, “I love to have my lust satisfied, and I cannot give it up.” And the gambler loves his sports, and cannot give them up. So they have become captive slaves to their flesh, and their very wilfulness has turned into helplessness; what they will not do, they say they cannot. And the worldling is so taken up with earthly things that he has neither heart, nor mind, nor time for heavenly ones. As in Pharaoh’s dream (Gen. 41:4), “the lean kine did eat up the fat ones,” so this lean and barren earth eats up all thoughts of heaven.

5. Some are so carried along by the stream of bad company that they are filled with hard thoughts of a godly life by hearing their companions speak against it; or at least they think they may risk doing what they see most people do, and so they keep on in their sinful ways. And when one of them is cut off and thrown into hell, and another snatched away from among them to the same condemnation, it does not much frighten them, because they do not see where they have gone. Poor wretches, they keep on in their ungodliness for all that, for they little know that their companions are now lamenting it in torment. In Luke 16, the rich man in hell would gladly have had someone warn his five brothers, so that they would not come to that place of torment. Probably he knew their minds and lives, and knew that they were hurrying there and little dreamed that he was there, and would hardly have believed anyone who told them so. I remember something a gentleman still living told me he saw on a bridge over the Severn. A man was driving a flock of fat lambs, and something met them and blocked their way. One of the lambs leaped onto the wall of the bridge, and, its legs slipping from under it, it fell into the river. The rest, seeing it, leaped over the bridge one after another, and all, or almost all, were drowned.—Those behind had little idea what had become of those that went before, but thought they could risk following their companions. But as soon as they were over the wall and falling headlong, it was a different matter. It is just the same with unconverted, carnal people. One dies beside them and drops into hell, and another follows the same way; and still they will go after them, because they do not think where they have gone. Oh, but when death has once opened their eyes and they see what is on the other side of the wall, in another world, what would they give to be back where they were!

6. Moreover, they have a cunning, malicious enemy whom they do not see, and who plays his game in the dark. His chief business is to hinder their conversion and so keep them where they are. He does it by persuading them not to believe the Scriptures, or not to trouble their minds with these matters; or by persuading them to think badly of a godly life, or to think it more fuss than is needed, and that they may be saved without conversion and without all this stir; and that God is so merciful that he will not damn people like them; or at least that they may stay a little longer, take their pleasure and follow the world a little longer yet, and then let it go and repent later. By deceitful tricks like these the devil keeps most people in his captivity and leads them to his misery. These and similar obstacles keep so many thousands unconverted, when God has done so much, Christ has suffered so much, and ministers have said so much for their conversion. When their reasons are silenced and they cannot answer the Lord who calls after them, “Turn ye, turn ye, why will ye die?”, it still all comes to nothing with most of them, and after all they leave us nothing to do but sit down and lament their wilful misery.

fields.title: Sermon IV
fields.body_html:
Ezek. 33:11.

Say to them, As I live, saith the Lord God, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live. Turn ye, turn ye, from your evil ways, for, why will ye die, O house of Israel?

I HAVE now shown you how reasonable God’s commands are, and how unreasonable the disobedience of wicked people is. If nothing will do, and people still refuse to turn, we must next consider whose fault it is if they are damned. And this brings me to the last doctrine, which is:

Doctrine 7. If, after all this, these people will not turn, it is not God’s fault that they are condemned, but their own, their own wilfulness. They die because they will die; that is, because they will not turn.

If you will go to hell, what remedy is there? God here clears himself of your blood; it will not be on him if you are lost. A negligent minister may bring it on himself, and those who encourage you in sin, or do not hinder you, may bring it on themselves; but be sure of this: it will not be on God. The Lord says of his unprofitable vineyard (Isa. 5:2, 3, 4), “Judge, I pray you, betwixt me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my vineyard, that I have not done in it?” When he had planted it in fruitful soil, fenced it, gathered out the stones and planted it with the choicest vines, what more should he have done to it? He has made you human beings and given you reason; he has supplied you with every outward necessity; he has given you a righteous, perfect law. When you had broken it and ruined yourselves, he had pity on you, and sent his Son, by a miracle of condescending mercy, to die for you and be a sacrifice for your sins; and he “was in Christ reconciling the world to himself.” The Lord Jesus has made you a deed of gift of himself, and of eternal life with him, on condition that you will only accept it and turn back. On this reasonable condition he has offered you the free pardon of all your sins. He has written this in his word, sealed it by his Spirit and sent it by his ministers. They have made you the offer (many times) and called you to accept it and turn to God. In his name they have pleaded with you, reasoned the case with you, and answered all your trivial objections. He has waited on you a long time, waited until you were ready, and put up with you abusing him to his face. He has mercifully sustained you in the middle of your sins. He has surrounded you with every kind of mercy, and has also mixed in afflictions to remind you of your folly and call you to your senses. And his Spirit has often striven with your hearts, saying there, “Turn, sinner, turn to the one who calls you. Where are you going? What are you doing? Do you know what the end will be? How long will you hate your friends and love your enemies? When will you let everything go, turn, give yourself up to God, and give your Redeemer possession of your soul? When will it ever be?” These pleas have been used with you. And when you have delayed, you have been urged to hurry, and God has called to you, “Today, while it is called today, harden not thy heart. Why not now, without any more delay?” Life has been set before you; the joys of heaven have been opened to you in the gospel; their certainty has been made plain; the certainty of the everlasting torments of the damned has been declared to you. Short of a sight of heaven and hell, what more could you want? Christ has been, as it were, set forth crucified before your eyes (Gal. 3:1). You have been told a hundred times that you are lost until you come to him. You have been told as often of the evil of sin; of the vanity of the world and all the pleasures and wealth it can give; of the shortness and uncertainty of your lives; and of the endless duration of the joy or torment of the life to come. All this, and more, you have been told, and told again, until you were tired of hearing it, and until you could make light of it because you had heard it so often, like the blacksmith’s dog that is brought by habit to sleep through the noise of the hammers, with the sparks flying round its ears. And though all this has not converted you, you are still alive, and could have mercy to this day if only you had hearts to receive it. Now let reason itself be the judge whether it is God’s fault or yours if, after this, you will stay unconverted and be damned. If you die now, it is because you will die. What more should be said to you? Or what course could be taken that is more likely to prevail? Can you say, and make it good, “We would gladly have been converted and become new creatures, but we could not; we would gladly have left our sins, but we could not; we would have changed our company, our thoughts and our conversation, but we could not”?—Why could you not, if you would? What hindered you but the wickedness of your hearts? Who forced you to sin, or who held you back from your duty? Did you not have the same teaching, time and freedom to be godly as your godly neighbours had? Why, then, could you not have been godly as well as they? Were the church doors shut against you? Or did you not stay away yourselves, or sit and sleep, or hear as if you did not hear? Did God make any exceptions against you in his word when he invited sinners to return and promised mercy to those who return? Did he say, “I will pardon all who repent except you”? Did he shut you out from the freedom of his holy worship? Did he forbid you to pray to him any more than others? You know he did not. God did not drive you away from him; you forsook him and ran away yourselves. And when he called you to himself, you would not come.—If God had left you out of the general promise and offer of mercy, or had said to you, “Stand back; I will have nothing to do with people like you; do not pray to me, for I will not hear you; however much you repent and cry for mercy, I will not regard you”; if God had left you nothing to rely on but despair, then you would have had a fair excuse. You might have said, “What is the point of repenting and turning, when it will do no good?”—But this was not your case. You could have had Christ to be your Lord and Saviour as well as others, and you would not; because you did not feel sick enough to need the physician, and because you could not spare your disease. In your hearts you said, like those rebels (Luke 19:14), “We will not have this man to reign over us.” Christ “would have gathered you under the wings of his salvation, and you would not” (Matt. 23:37). What desires for your welfare the Lord expressed in his holy word! With what compassion he stood over you and said, “O that my people had hearkened unto me, and that they had walked in my ways!” (Psa. 81:13). “O that there were such an heart in them, that they would fear me, and keep all my commandments always, that it might be well with them, and with their children for ever!” (Deut. 5:29). “O that they were wise, that they understood this, that they would consider their latter end!” (Deut. 32:29). He would have been your God and done everything for you that your souls could rightly desire; but you loved the world and your flesh more than him, and so you would not listen to him. Though you paid him compliments and gave him high titles, when it came to closing the bargain “you would have none of him” (Psa. 81:11, 12). “No wonder, then, if he gave you up to your own lusts, and you walked in your own counsels.”—He stoops to reason and pleads the case with you, and asks you, “What is there in me or my service that you should be so much against me? What harm have I done you, sinner? Have I deserved this unkind treatment from you? I have shown you many mercies; for which of them do you despise me like this? Is it I or Satan who is your enemy? Is it I or your carnal self that would ruin you? Is it a holy life or a life of sin that you have reason to flee from? If you are ruined, you bring it on yourself by forsaking me, the Lord, who would have saved you” (Jer. 2:17). “Thine own wickedness shall correct thee, and thy backslidings shall reprove thee: know therefore and see that it is an evil thing and bitter, that thou hast forsaken the Lord thy God” (Jer. 2:19). “What iniquity have your fathers found in me, that they are gone far from me, and have walked after vanity?” (Jer. 2:5, 6). He calls out, as it were, to the inanimate creation to hear the dispute he has with you (Micah 6:2, 3, 4): “Hear ye, O mountains, the Lord’s controversy, and ye strong foundations of the earth: for the Lord hath a controversy with his people, and he will plead with Israel. O my people, what have I done unto thee? and wherein have I wearied thee? testify against me. For I brought thee up out of the land of Egypt, and redeemed thee,” and so on. “Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth: for the Lord hath spoken, I have nourished and brought up children, and they have rebelled against me. The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master’s crib: but Israel doth not know, my people doth not consider. Ah sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, a seed of evildoers,” and so on (Isa. 1:2, 3, 4). “Do ye thus requite the Lord, O foolish people and unwise? is not he thy father that hath bought thee? hath he not made thee, and established thee?” (Deut. 32:6). When he saw that you forsook him for nothing at all, and turned away from your Lord and your life to hunt after the chaff and feathers of the world, he told you of your folly and called you to more profitable work (Isa. 55:1, 2, 3): “Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness. Incline your ear, and come unto me: hear, and your soul shall live; and I will make an everlasting covenant with you, even the sure mercies of David.—Seek ye the Lord while he may be found, call ye upon him while he is near: let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the Lord, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon” (verses 6, 7); and so also Isa. 1:16, 17, 18. And when you would not listen, what complaints you have driven him to, charging it on you as your wilfulness and stubbornness!—Jer. 2:12, 13: “Be astonished, O ye heavens, at this, and be horribly afraid!—For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.”—Many times Christ has proclaimed that free invitation to you (Rev. 22:17): “Let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely.” But after all his offers you drove him to complain, “Ye will not come to me, that ye might have life” (John 5:40). He has invited you to feast with him in the kingdom of his grace, and you have made excuses about your fields, your cattle and your worldly business; and when you would not come, you said you could not, and provoked him to resolve that you should never taste of his supper (Luke 14:15, 24). And whose fault is it now but your own? And what can we say is the chief cause of your damnation but your own wills? You will be damned. The whole case is laid open by Christ himself in Proverbs 1, from verse 20 to the end: “Wisdom crieth without; she uttereth her voice in the streets: she crieth in the chief place of concourse: How long, ye simple ones, will ye love simplicity? and the scorners delight in their scorning, and fools hate knowledge? Turn you at my reproof: behold, I will pour out my spirit unto you, I will make known my words unto you. Because I have called, and ye refused; I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded; but ye have set at nought all my counsel, and would none of my reproof: I also will laugh at your calamity; I will mock when your fear cometh; when your fear cometh as desolation, and your destruction cometh as a whirlwind; when distress and anguish cometh upon you. Then shall they call upon me, but I will not answer; they shall seek me early, but they shall not find me: for that they hated knowledge, and did not choose the fear of the Lord: they would none of my counsel: they despised all my reproof. Therefore shall they eat of the fruit of their own way, and be filled with their own devices. For the turning away of the simple shall slay them, and the prosperity of fools shall destroy them. But whoso hearkeneth unto me shall dwell safely, and shall be quiet from fear of evil.”—I thought it best to quote the whole text to you in full, because it shows so fully the cause of the destruction of the wicked. It is not because God would not teach them, but because they would not learn. It is not because God would not call them, but because they would not turn at his reproof. Their wilfulness is their ruin.

USE.

From what has been said, you may further learn the following things.

1. From this you may see not only what blasphemy and ungodliness it is to lay the blame for people’s destruction on God, but also how unfit these wicked wretches are to bring such a charge against their Maker. They cry out against God and say he does not give them grace, that his threats are severe, and God forbid that all who are not converted and sanctified should be damned. They think it hard treatment that a short sin should bring endless suffering, and if they are damned they say they cannot help it; while all the time they are busy with their own destruction, cutting the throats of their own souls, and will not be persuaded to hold back their hands. They think God would be cruel if he damned them; and yet they are so cruel to themselves that they will run into the fire of hell when God has told them it lies just ahead of them, and neither pleading nor threats nor anything that can be said will stop them. We see them nearly ruined; their careless, worldly, fleshly lives tell us that they are in the power of the devil. We know that if they die before they are converted, all the world cannot save them; and knowing how uncertain their lives are, we are afraid every day that they will drop into the fire. So we plead with them to pity their own souls and not ruin themselves when mercy is at hand, and they will not listen to us. We plead with them to throw away their sin and come to Christ without delay, and to have some mercy on themselves; but they will have none. And yet they think God must be cruel if he condemns them. O wilful, miserable sinners! It is not God who is cruel to you; it is you who are cruel to yourselves. You are told that you must turn or burn, and still you do not turn. You are told that if you insist on keeping your sins, you will keep the curse of God with them, and still you will keep them. You are told that there is no way to happiness except by holiness, and still you will not be holy. What more would you have God say to you? What would you have him do with his mercy? He offers it to you, and you will not have it. You are in the ditch of sin and misery, and he would give you his hand to help you out, and you refuse his help. He would cleanse you of your sins, and you would rather keep them. You love your lust, your gluttony, your sports and your drunkenness, and will not let them go. Would you have him bring you to heaven whether you want to go or not? Or would you have him bring you and your sins to heaven together? That is an impossibility; you might as well expect him to turn the sun into darkness. What! An unsanctified, fleshly heart in heaven! It cannot be. “There shall in no wise enter into it any thing that defileth” (Rev. 21:27). “For what communion hath light with darkness? And what concord hath Christ with Belial?” (2 Cor. 6:14, 15). “All day long I have stretched forth my hands unto a disobedient and gainsaying people” (Rom. 10:21). What will you do now? Will you cry to God for mercy? God calls on you to have mercy on yourselves, and you will not. Ministers see the poisoned cup in the drunkard’s hand, tell him there is poison in it, and beg him to have mercy on his soul and hold back; and he will not listen to us. Drink it he must and will; he loves it; and so, though hell comes next, he says he cannot help it. What should one say to people like this? We tell the ungodly, careless worldling that such a life will not do, nor ever bring him to heaven. If a bear were at your back, you would quicken your pace; and when the curse of God is at your back, and Satan and hell are at your back, will you not move, but ask, What is the need for all this fuss? Is an immortal soul worth no more than that? Oh, have mercy on yourselves! But they will have no mercy on themselves, nor pay us the least attention. We tell them the end will be bitter: who can live with the everlasting fire? And still they will have no mercy on themselves. And yet these poor wretches will say that God is too merciful to condemn them, when it is they themselves who cruelly and unmercifully rush on condemnation; and if we go to them and plead with them, we cannot stop them. If we fell on our knees to them, we could not stop them; to hell they will go, and still will not believe that they are going there. If we beg them, for the sake of God who made them and preserves them, for the sake of Christ who died for them, for the sake of their own poor souls, to pity themselves and go no further on the road to hell, but to come to Christ while his arms are open, enter the state of life while the door stands open, and take mercy now while mercy may be had, they will not be persuaded. If it cost us our lives, we could not get them even to think the matter over with themselves now and then, and turn. And still they can say, “I hope God will be merciful.” Did you never consider what he says in Isa. 27:11: “It is a people of no understanding: therefore he that made them will not have mercy on them, and he that formed them will shew them no favour”? If another person will not clothe you when you are naked and feed you when you are hungry, you say he is unmerciful. If he threw you into prison, or beat and tormented you, you would say he is unmerciful. And yet you will do a thousand times more against yourselves, even throw away both soul and body for ever, and never complain of your own unmercifulness! And God, who waited on you with his mercy all that while, must be considered unmerciful if he punishes you after all this. Unless the holy God of heaven lets these wretches trample on his Son’s blood, and, like the Jews, spit in his face again, as it were, do despite to the Spirit of grace, make a joke of sin and a mockery of holiness, and think less of saving mercy than of the filth of their fleshly pleasures; and unless after all this he saves them by the mercy they threw away and would have none of, God himself must be called unmerciful by them.—But he will be justified when he judges, and he will not stand or fall at the bar of a sinful worm.—I know many particular quibbles are brought against the Lord by them; but I will not stop here to answer them one by one, having done so already in my Treatise of Judgment, to which I refer them. If the arguing part of the world had been as careful to avoid sin and destruction as they have been busy searching for its causes and quick to blame them directly on God, they might have used their wits more profitably, wronged God less, and done better for themselves. When so ugly a monster as sin is within us, so heavy a thing as punishment is on us, and so dreadful a thing as hell is before us, one would think it an easy question who is at fault, whether God or man is the principal or blameworthy cause. Some people are such lenient judges of themselves that they are quicker to accuse infinite perfection and goodness itself than their own hearts. They imitate their first parents, who said, “The serpent beguiled me, and the woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat,” secretly implying that God was the cause. So they say, “The understanding you gave me was unable to discern; the will you gave me was unable to make a better choice; the things you set before me enticed me; the temptation you allowed to attack me prevailed against me.” And some are so unwilling to think that God can make a self-determining creature that they dare not deny him what they take to be his prerogative, to be the determiner of the will in every sin, as its first, efficient, immediate, physical cause.—And many would be content to clear God of so much causing of evil, if only they could reconcile it with his being the chief cause of good; as if truths would no longer be truths if we cannot see them in their perfect order and connection. Because our tangled wits cannot see them properly together, or assign each truth its proper place, we presume to conclude that some must be thrown away. This is the fruit of proud self-conceit, when people do not receive God’s truth as a child receives his lesson, in holy submission to the all-knowing Teacher, but as critics who are too wise to learn.

Objection. But we cannot convert ourselves until God converts us; we can do nothing without his grace. It is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.

Answer. God has two degrees of mercy to show: the mercy of conversion first, and the mercy of salvation last. The latter he will give to no one but those who will and run, and he has promised it to them only. The former is to make those willing who are unwilling. And though your own willingness and efforts do not deserve his grace, your wilful refusal does deserve that it should be denied you. Your inability is your very unwillingness itself, which does not excuse your sin but makes it greater. You could turn if only you were truly willing. And if your wills themselves are so corrupted that nothing but effectual grace will move them, you have all the more reason to seek that grace and yield to it, and to do what you can in using the means, and not neglect it or set yourself against it. Do what you are able to do first, and then complain of God for denying you grace, if you have reason to.

Objection. But you seem to imply all this while that man has free will.

Answer. The dispute about free will is beyond your capacity, so I will trouble you now with no more about it than this. Your will is by nature a free, that is, a self-determining, faculty; but it is wickedly inclined and reluctant to do good, and so we see by sad experience that it does not have a virtuous moral freedom. But it is its wickedness that deserves the punishment. And I beg you, let us not make fools of ourselves with opinions. Make the case your own. If you had an enemy so malicious that he attacked you and beat you every time he met you, and took the lives of your children, would you excuse him because he said, “I do not have free will; it is my nature; I cannot choose otherwise unless God gives me grace”? If you had a servant who robbed you, would you accept such an answer from him? Could not every thief and murderer hanged at the assizes give such an answer: “I do not have free will; I cannot change my own heart! What can I do without God’s grace?” And should they be acquitted for that? If not, why should you think you will be acquitted for a course of sin against the Lord?

2. From this you may also observe these three things together: 1. what a cunning tempter Satan is; 2. what a deceitful thing sin is; 3. what a foolish creature corrupted man is. A cunning tempter indeed, who can persuade the greater part of the world to go deliberately into everlasting fire when they have so many warnings and dissuasions! A deceitful thing indeed is sin, which can bewitch so many thousands into parting with everlasting life for something so low and utterly worthless! A foolish creature indeed is man, who will be cheated out of his salvation for nothing, indeed for a nothing he knows to be nothing, and by an enemy, and an enemy he knows! You would think it impossible for anyone in his right mind to be persuaded, for a trifle, to throw himself into fire or water or a coal pit, to the destruction of his life. And yet people will be enticed into throwing themselves into hell. If your natural lives were in your own hands, so that you would not die until you killed yourselves, how long would most of you live? And yet, when your everlasting life is so far in your own hands, under God, that you cannot be ruined until you ruin yourselves, how few of you will hold back from your own ruin! Ah, what a foolish thing man is! And what a bewitching, befooling thing sin is!

3. From this you may also learn that it is no great wonder if wicked people hinder others on the way to heaven, want as many unconverted as they can get, and try to draw them into sin and keep them in it! Can you expect those who have no mercy on themselves to have mercy on others? Or that those who do not hesitate to destroy themselves should hesitate much over the destruction of others? They do no worse to others than they do to themselves.

4. Lastly, you may learn from this that man’s greatest enemy is himself; that the greatest judgment that can come on him in this life is to be left to himself; that the great work grace has to do is to save us from ourselves; that people’s greatest accusations and complaints should be against themselves; that the greatest work we have to do ourselves is to resist ourselves; that the greatest enemy we should pray and watch and strive against every day is our own carnal hearts and wills; and that the greatest part of your work, if you want to do good to others and help them to heaven, is to save them from themselves: from their blind understandings, corrupted wills, perverse affections, violent passions and unruly senses. I only name all these for brevity’s sake, and leave them for your further consideration.

WELL, Sirs, now that we have found the great offender and murderer of souls (people’s own selves, their own wills), what remains but for you to judge according to the evidence, confess this great iniquity before the Lord, be humbled for it, and do it no more? For these three ends in turn I will add a few more words: 1. to convince you further; 2. to humble you; and 3. to reform you, if there is still any hope.

1. We know so much of the exceedingly gracious nature of God, who is so willing to do good and delights to show mercy, that we have no reason to suspect him of being the blameworthy cause of our death, or to call him cruel. He has made all things good, and he preserves and maintains them all. “The eyes of all wait upon thee; and thou givest them their meat in due season. Thou openest thine hand, and satisfiest the desire of every living thing” (Psa. 145:15, 16). He is not only “righteous in all his ways” (and so will deal justly) “and holy in all his works” (and so is not the author of sin), but he is also “good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works” (Psa. 145:17, 9). But as for man, we know that his mind is dark, his will perverse, and his affections carry him so headlong that by his folly and corruption he is suited to such a work as destroying himself. If you saw a lamb lying killed on the road, would you sooner suspect the sheep or the wolf of doing it, if both were standing by? Or if you saw a house broken into and the people murdered, would you sooner suspect the prince or judge, who is wise and just and had no need to, or a known thief or murderer? So I say, as in James 1:13, 14, 15: “Let no man say when he is tempted, I am tempted of God: for God cannot be tempted with evil, neither tempteth he any man” (to draw him to sin): “but every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed. Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death.” You see here that sin is the offspring of your own lust, and is not to be fathered on God; and that death is the offspring of your own sin, the fruit it will yield you as soon as it is ripe. You have a store of evil in yourselves, as a spider has of poison, from which you are producing harm to yourselves and spinning webs that entangle your own souls. Your nature shows that it is you who are the cause.

2. It is plain that you are your own destroyers, because you are so ready to welcome almost any temptation that is offered to you. Satan is hardly more ready to move you to any evil than you are to listen and do what he wants. If he tempts your understanding to error and prejudice, you give in. If he wants to keep you from good resolutions, it is soon done. If he wants to cool any good desires or affections, it is soon done. If he wants to kindle any lust or vile affections and desires in you, it is soon done. If he wants to push you into evil thoughts or deeds, you are so willing that he needs neither whip nor spur. If he wants to keep you from holy thoughts and words and ways, a little does it; you need no bridle. You do not examine his suggestions, nor resist them with any resolve, nor throw them out as he throws them in, nor put out the sparks he tries to kindle. You join in with him, meet him halfway, embrace his suggestions and tempt him to tempt you. And it is easy for him to catch such greedy fish, which are roaming about for bait and will take the bare hook.

3. Your destruction plainly comes from yourselves, because you resist everything that would help to save you, do you good, or keep you from ruining yourselves. God would help and save you by his word, and you resist it; it is too strict for you. He would sanctify you by his Spirit, and you resist and quench it. If anyone rebukes you for your sin, you fly in his face with harsh words; and if he would draw you to a holy life and tell you of your present danger, you give him little thanks, but either tell him to mind himself, since he will not have to answer for you, or at best put him off with heartless thanks, and will not turn even when you are persuaded. If ministers would instruct and help you privately, you will not come to them; your unhumbled souls feel little need of their help. If they would catechise you, you are too old to be catechised, though you are not too old to be ignorant and unholy. Whatever they can say to you for your good, you are so conceited and wise in your own eyes (even in the depths of ignorance) that you will pay no attention to anything that does not agree with your present notions, but contradict your teachers as if you were wiser than they. You resist all they can say to you by your ignorance, wilfulness, foolish quibbles, slippery evasions and ungrateful rejections; so no good that is offered can find any welcome or reception with you.

4. Moreover, it is plain that you are self-destroyers, because you draw the material for your sin and destruction even from the blessed God himself. You do not like the design of his wisdom. You do not like his justice, but take it for cruelty. You do not like his holiness, but are ready to think he is altogether such a one as yourselves (Psa. 50:21) and makes as light of sin as you do. You do not like his truth, but would have his threats, even his absolute threats, prove false. And his goodness, which you seem to approve most highly, you partly resist, as it would lead you to repentance, and partly abuse to strengthen your sin, as if you might sin freely because God is merciful and because his grace abounds so much.

5. Indeed, you draw destruction from the blessed Redeemer, and death from the Lord of life himself! Nothing makes you bolder in sin than that Christ has died for you; as if the danger of death were now over and you could venture boldly; as if Christ had become a servant to Satan and your sins, and must wait on you while you are abusing him. And because he has become the physician of souls, and is able to save to the uttermost all who come to God by him, you think he must let you refuse his help and throw away his medicines, and must save you whether you come to God by him or not. So a great part of your sins comes from your bold presumption on the death of Christ, not considering that he came to redeem his people from their sins, to sanctify them as a special people for himself, and to conform them in holiness to the image of their heavenly Father and of their Head (Matt. 1:21; Titus 2:14; 1 Pet. 1:15, 16; Col. 3:10, 11; Phil. 3:9, 10).

6. You also draw your own destruction from all the providences and works of God. When you think of his eternal foreknowledge and decrees, it is to harden you in your sin or fill your minds with quarrelsome thoughts, as if his decrees could spare you the trouble of repentance and a holy life, or else were the cause of sin and death. If he afflicts you, you complain; if he prospers you, you forget him all the more and are all the more reluctant to think of the life to come. If the wicked prosper, you forget the end that will settle all accounts, and are ready to think it is as good to be wicked as godly. And so you draw your death from everything.

7. You do the same with all God’s creatures and mercies to you. He gives them to you as tokens of his love and equipment for his service, and you turn them against him to please your flesh. You eat and drink to please your appetite, and not for the glory of God or to enable you to do his work. You abuse your clothes for pride. Your riches draw your hearts away from heaven (Phil. 3:18). Your honours and applause puff you up. If you have wealth and strength, it makes you more complacent and forgetful of your end. Indeed, you abuse other people’s mercies to your own harm. If you see their honours and rank, you are provoked to envy them. If you see their riches, you are ready to covet them. If you look on beauty, you are stirred up to lust. And it is well if godliness itself is not an eyesore to you.

8. The very gifts God gives you, and the ordinances of grace he has instituted for his church, you turn into sin. If you have better abilities than others, you grow proud and conceited. If you have only common gifts, you take them for special grace. You take merely hearing your duty to be so good a work that it would excuse you for not obeying it. Your prayers are turned into sin, because you regard iniquity in your hearts (Psa. 66:18), and do not “depart from iniquity” when you “name the name of Christ” (2 Tim. 2:19). Your prayers are abominable, because you “turn away your ear from hearing the law” (Prov. 28:9), and are more ready “to give the sacrifice of fools” (thinking you do God some special service) than to hear his word and obey it (Eccles. 5:1).

9. Indeed, you make the people you mix with, and all their actions, the occasions of your sin and destruction. If they live in the fear of God, you hate them.—If they live ungodly lives, you imitate them. If the wicked are many, you think you can follow them more boldly. If the godly are few, you are bolder in despising them. If they live carefully, you think they are too strict. If one of them falls in some particular temptation, you stumble over them and turn away from holiness because others are imperfectly holy; as if you were entitled to break your necks because some others, through carelessness, have sprained a muscle or put out a joint. If a hypocrite exposes himself, you say they are all alike, and think yourselves just as honest. A professing Christian can hardly slip into any wrongdoing but, because he cuts his finger, you think you may boldly cut your throats. If ministers deal plainly with you, you say they rail. If they speak gently or coolly, you either sleep under them or are hardly more moved than the seats you sit on. If any errors creep into the church, some eagerly embrace them, and others blame Christian doctrine for them, which is most against them. And if we try to draw you away from some ancient, deep-rooted error that can claim two, three, six or seven hundred years of custom, you are as offended by a proposal for reform as if it would cost you your life, and you hold fast to old errors while you cry out against new ones. Hardly any disagreement can arise among the ministers of the gospel without your drawing your own death from it. And you will not hear, or at least not obey, the unquestionable teaching of any of them who do not fall in with your notions. One will not hear a minister because he says the Lord’s Prayer, and another will not hear him because he does not use it. One will not hear those who are for episcopacy, and another will not hear those who are against it. And so I could show you in many other cases how you turn everything that comes near you to your own destruction; so clear is it that the ungodly are self-destroyers, and that their ruin is of their own making.

I think that now, on considering what has been said and reviewing your own ways, you should think about what you have done, and be ashamed and deeply humbled to remember it. If you are not, I beg you to consider the following truths.

1. To be your own destroyers is to sin against the deepest principle of your nature, the principle of self-preservation. Everything naturally desires or inclines towards its own happiness, welfare or perfection. And will you set yourselves to work your own destruction? When you are commanded to love your neighbours as yourselves, it is assumed that you naturally love yourselves. But if you love your neighbours no better than yourselves, it seems you would have all the world damned.

2. How completely you defeat your own intentions! I know you do not intend your own damnation, even while you are bringing it about. You think you are only doing yourselves good by satisfying the desires of your flesh. But alas! It is only like a drink of cold water in a burning fever, or like scratching an itching rash, which makes the disease and the pain worse. If you really want pleasure, profit or honour, seek them where they are to be found, and do not hunt for them on the road to hell.

3. What a pity it is that you should do against yourselves what no one else on earth or in hell can do! If all the world, or all the devils in hell, were joined against you, they could not destroy you without you, nor make you sin without your own consent. And will you do against yourselves what no one else can do? You have hateful thoughts of the devil because he is your enemy and tries to destroy you. And will you be worse than devils to yourselves?
